papers.title: Synergising local geo-environmental characteristics with spatial context for enhancing landslide susceptibility mapping
papers.summary: Data-driven methods are widely used in landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) because they can effectively model the complex relationships between landslides and geo-environmental conditions. Existing data-driven approaches generally follow two types of data representations. Pixel-based models focus solely on the geo-environmental characteristics of a specific landslide but neglect the influence of its surrounding environment. Patch-based models incorporate surrounding spatial context but may include pixels with weak or no spatial relevance to the target landslide location. To address this limitation, this study proposes a Local-Geo and Spatial Context Fusion (LGSCF) strategy, which synergises the geo-environmental characteristics of landslide points with their corresponding spatial context through a feature-wise modulation mechanism. We tested the LGSCF strategy by integrating it into several representative convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, creating nine different LGSCF-based models. The primary study area covers approximately 2644 km² across Jenai and Sinyi Townships in Nantou County, Taiwan, and the dataset comprises 5332 landslide samples and an equal number of non-landslide samples. The results show that LGSCF-based models consistently outperform their corresponding baselines, achieving F1-scores up to 87.09% and AUC values up to 0.9472. Furthermore, the susceptibility maps produced by LGSCF-based models show that known landslides are more accurately concentrated in “very high” susceptibility zones with fewer misclassifications. These findings demonstrate that our fusion strategy can significantly improve the accuracy of landslide susceptibility mapping.

papers.summary: BigLeak Archaeology BigLeak Archaeology V1.3 – A Formally Falsifiable Compression Protocol for Symbolic Systems This independent research document tests the hypothesis of a domain-general cognitive compression protocol underlying prehistoric symbolic clusters. We define a 5-slot essence E = {σ Origin, κ Relation, π Individuation, τ Time, γ Transition} and operationalize compliance through four explicit axioms: |E|=5, E⊂V, |V|≥13 (implements |V|/|E|≥2.5), and S(E)/S(V) ∈ [0.6;0.7]. Entropy calculations, codebook V1-V4 and a runnable Python evaluator are included for full reproducibility (Cohen K_IRR = 0.72). N=15 symbolic clusters from 18,000 BP to 1000 AD across four continents pass all axioms; a contrast sample of 4 complex structures passes 0/4, demonstrating discriminant validity. After quantitative taphonomic analysis (infinite-slope Factor of Safety FS=1.38-1.96 = marginally stable, ∼100% noise), the originally preregistered test case Göbekli Tepe Enclosure F is retained as control. Primary is now the landslide-resilient Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum, Malta (FS≈183.6, <1% noise, carved from in situ limestone bedrock), with Chauvet Cave and Yazılıkaya as secondary / tertiary. papers.title: Initiation thresholds and statistical properties of rainfall-induced landslides under centennial-scale variations in land use and land cover and rainfall characteristics
AI-based procedure for extracting spatial and temporal information on rainfall-induced landslides from textual sources
papers.summary: Abstract Comprehensive landslide catalogues require accurate and reproducible spatial and temporal information, yet manual extraction from textual sources is time-consuming and affected by inter- and intra-operator variability. We present AIDE4LAND (Artificial Intelligence-based procedure for Data Extraction for LANDslides), a novel structured procedure that combines Large Language Models and prompt engineering to automatically extract temporal and spatial information on rainfall-induced landslides from textual sources. The procedure is organized as a two-step process: (i) temporal extraction, which reconstructs the date and time of occurrence according to explicit hierarchical rules and assigns standardized temporal accuracy levels, and (ii) spatial extraction, which progressively determines geographic coordinates through structured queries and reverse-geocoding validation using OpenStreetMap APIs via Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol. The workflow was developed through iterative prompt-refinement cycles, involving 2162 tests conducted on 725 textual sources (664 written in Italian and 61 in English) published between 2011 and 2025. Validation of AIDE4LAND outputs against a manually compiled expert dataset revealed a high level of agreement, with 87% of cases demonstrating maximum concordance in terms of temporal and spatial attribution. By combining standardized rules, explicit accuracy classification, and automated consistency checks, AIDE4LAND formalizes expert reasoning into transparent and reproducible procedural rules, thereby reducing interpretative variability and ensuring transparent and systematic traceability in the decision process. The procedure significantly accelerates catalogue updates and provides a transferable and reproducible methodological framework for constructing structured rainfall-induced landslide catalogues, supporting hazard assessment, rainfall-threshold definition, and early warning applications.

papers.title: Guangdong rainfall-induced landslide inventory and environmental variables for latent-regime analysis
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This dataset contains the processed research data supporting the study “Latent infiltration regimes mediate environmental controls on delayed rainfall-induced landslides.” The dataset comprises 2,025 rainfall-related landslide records from Guangdong Province, South China, together with the environmental variables used to investigate delayed landslide responses to rainfall forcing. The dataset includes landslide identifiers and locations, occurrence and rainfall-event timing information, landslide lag time, soil thickness, slope, aspect, lithology, and antecedent cumulative rainfall over 3-h, 6-h, 12-h, 1-day, 2-day, and 3-day windows. Figure-level data and model-output files used to evaluate the analyses reported in the manuscript are also provided. The dataset supports the statistical analyses, Bayesian latent-regime inference, model selection, environmental attribution, and figure generation presented in the manuscript. A data dictionary describing the variables, units, and processing information is included in the archive. Original third-party source records subject to redistribution restrictions are not redistributed in this archive. Their provenance and access conditions are documented in the accompanying documentation.

papers.title: Forensic back-analysis of a reactivated deep-seated landslide in volcanic residual soils of the Cisumdawu highway KM 178, Indonesia
papers.summary: Abstract Background This study is a forensic back-analysis of the 2021 embankment failure at KM 178 of the Cisumdawu Highway, Indonesia. The post-failure investigation identified weak subsurface materials but no discrete failure horizon, and the mechanism was never established. Six independent lines of field evidence were assembled, from UAV LiDAR geomorphology to paired triaxial and direct shear testing. A two-dimensional Morgenstern–Price model was built with the failure surface fixed from that evidence while material parameters were calibrated. Pore pressure was represented as a material-specific ratio rather than a piezometric surface, the residual soil permeability being too low to transmit storm rainfall to depth. Uncertainty was propagated by Monte Carlo simulation. Results The alignment crosses a valley floored by relict landslide deposits, with arcuate paleo-scarps on the upper slope. The weathering profile grades from residual silty clay through residual silty sand to weathered tuff, placing a granular horizon within low-permeability clay, so permeability is not monotonic with depth. Inclinometers installed after the rupture intercepted a shear horizon at 559 and 536 m elevation, recording 15 cm and 10 cm of cumulative wet-season displacement, while the instrument monitored during the dry season recorded none. Deeper horizons remain active but could not be traced laterally, indicating a larger relict complex. That horizon coincides with N-SPT below 10 enclosed within material returning 20 to 30, a strength inversion weathering cannot produce, and with gravelly deposits of low resistivity. Without imposed pore pressure it is not the critical surface, returning 1.40 against 1.29 for a shallower surface within the embankment. It becomes critical only when the pore-pressure ratio reaches about 0.37, at an operational friction angle of 20.5°, below the measured peak of 29°. Peer Review Report For: Physical and Mechanical Characteristics of Soil as a Controlling Factor in Landslides in Curug Panjang Village, Cihuni Hamlet, Lebak, Banten: Analysis of Distribution, Normality, and Inter-parameter Relationships [version 2; peer review: 1 approved, 1 approved with reservations]
papers.summary: Background Landslide occurrence is strongly influenced by the physical and mechanical properties of subsurface soil; this study evaluates these properties in residual soil from Kampung Cihuni, Lebak Regency, as a controlling factor in landslides. Methods Thirty residual soil samples were collected at a depth of 0–1 m using a grid sampling method. Laboratory testing covered natural water content (w); specific gravity and unit weight, used to derive void ratio (e); the plasticity index (PI) from the Atterberg limits; and Unconsolidated Undrained (UU) triaxial testing for cohesion (c) and internal friction angle (φ). The distribution of each parameter was evaluated using histograms, Q-Q plots, and the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, while inter-parameter relationships were analysed using linear regression (R 2 ) and Spearman correlation (ρ). Results The Shapiro-Wilk test showed that cohesion (c) and void ratio (e) are normally distributed, whereas water content (w), PI, and friction angle (φ) are not. PI values for the plastic samples (n = 26) ranged from 13.8% to 86.7%, and φ ranged from 5.48° to 20.5°; the relationship between the two was weakly positive (R 2 = 0.151, p = 0.050; Spearman ρ = 0.244, p = 0.229). Cohesion ranged from 4.41–52.47 kPa but showed a very weak, non-significant relationship with water content (R 2 = 0.028, p = 0.376), as did void ratio with φ (R 2 = 0.089, p = 0.110). Conclusions Relationships among the physical and mechanical parameters were weak and mostly non-significant, so the reduction in soil shear strength cannot be explained by any single parameter alone. Because the UU triaxial test represents total-stress conditions, it cannot directly explain rainfall infiltration and pore-water pressure change as a landslide trigger, though it offers an initial picture of the residual soil’s engineering characteristics as a controlling factor in the area’s landslide susceptibility.

papers.title: Permafrost Monitoring in the Central Alaska Network of National Parks
papers.summary: The three national park units which comprise the National Park Service Inventory and Monitoring Program’s Central Alaska Network (CAKN: Wrangell-St. Elias, Denali, and Yukon-Charley Rivers) are underlain by permafrost—ground that remains at or below 0°C for at least two, but typically many, years. Much of that permafrost, however, is geographically discontinuous, thin, and close to the melting point of water. Under the warming conditions that characterize these parks, permafrost thaw is likely to have significant impacts on the landscapes of these parks. These impacts may include development of thermokarst, landslides and slumping, changes in hydrology and vegetation, growth and/or drainage of lakes, enhanced release of greenhouse gases, and decay of characteristic permafrost features like pingos and rock glaciers. The CAKN permafrost monitoring program is designed to monitor a subset of these changes over multiple decades, and focuses on tracking changes in the thermal and physical state of permafrost. Collected data will contribute directly to the Global Terrestrial Network for Permafrost, the primary international permafrost monitoring program. Thermal changes will be monitored with a broad network of shallow (<3 m) soil temperature measurements, and also with temperature measurements from a single deep (29-70 m) borehole adjacent to each park. These measurements will mostly be conducted in collaboration with existing monitoring programs to leverage existing resources. Physical changes will be monitored with a network of active layer thickness measurements that use late-summer mechanical probing to determine maximum thaw depth on fine-grained permafrost soils. The thaw depth measurements will be co-located with survey-grade differential global positioning system (dGPS) surveys of soil surface elevation to detect thaw-related subsidence. papers.title: Integrating Kernel-Based Machine Learning Techniques with Geospatial Analysis for Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in Sikkim, India
papers.source: Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering
papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards, causing substantial loss of life and infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions. Accurate identification of landslide-prone areas remains challenging due to complex and nonlinear interactions among geological, topographical, and environmental factors. This study evaluates kernel-based machine learning approaches, namely, kernel logistic regression (KLR) and support vector machine (SVM), for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) in Sikkim, India. A balanced data set comprising 693 landslide and 695 nonlandslide samples was constructed using 15 conditioning factors representing topographic, hydrological, environmental, geological, and seismic conditions. The grid search method was utilized to identify optimal hyperparameter configurations. Model performance was quantitatively assessed using accuracy, kappa coefficient, specificity, area under curve (AUC), landslide density, and success rate curve (SRC). The results demonstrate that the KLR with a polynomial kernel (KLR_poly) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.741 and an area under curve (AUC) of 0.829, outperforming other KLR variants, while the SVM with an rbf kernel (SVM_rbf) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.749 and an AUC of 0.764, outperforming other SVM variants. Furthermore, the landslide density analysis showed a systematic increase in landslide concentration from low to high susceptibility classes for nonlinear models, while SRC results indicated moderate to good predictive capability across all models, confirming effective spatial prioritization of landslide-prone areas. Additionally, a feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most significant factors influencing landslide occurrence.

papers.title: Spatial machine learning modelling reveals that soil indicators and tree type best explain shallow landslide release
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: The exploration of shallow landslide susceptibility is often impaired by biased landslide inventories, and by over-optimistic performance metrics linked to inadequate models. Here, we use a systematically mapped event inventory of 571 shallow landslides triggered in southern Norway and apply 32 gradient boosted decision tree models to rigorously test the effects of (1) a nested vs. simple cross-validation strategy, (2) spatial vs. non-spatial models, (3) four different cross-validation sampling strategies which were applied on (4) full vs. forest-only datasets. Model evaluation shows that models with random cross-validation provided the highest test performance metrics but did not account for autocorrelation and were likely over-optimistic. The spatial models with spatial cross-validation reduced autocorrelation in the model residuals at the expense of predictive power. Although no model emerged as optimal, findings across models suggest that important explanatory factors like elevation, aspect and bedrock weatherability serve as soil indicators, illustrating a need for improved datasets for soil thickness and heterogeneity. In the forest-only models, tree type was consistently an important predictor, with higher landslide susceptibility in deciduous forest, illustrating the potential of forest variables and forest-specific threshold values in shallow landslide susceptibility mapping.

papers.title: Silent forces rising risks: A systematic review of natural hazards, cascading processes and emerging risk in the Himalaya
papers.source: International Journal of Geography Geology and Environment
papers.summary: Background: The Himalaya is the youngest, highest and most tectonically and climatically active mountain belt on Earth. Hazard prone environments create by large human populations. Traditionally, earthquakes, rainfall- and earthquake triggered landslides, debris flows, glacial lake outburst floods (GLOF), permafrost degradation, rock ice avalanches and snow avalanches have been studied as separate hazard classes. Yet field evidence from recent disasters shows that these events are frequently linked in cascading and compounding sequences. Objective: This review synthesizes peer-reviewed and institutional literature on natural hazards and emerging cascading risk across the Himalayan arc with emphasis on (i) the geological and climatic drivers of individual hazard types (ii) documented cascading and compound hazard pathways, (iii) the growing exposure of settlements and infrastructure and (iv) research and risk management gaps. Methods: A structured systematic literature review was undertaken. Academic search platforms (Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Wiley Online Library, Nature Portfolio journals, Copernicus/NHESS, MDPI, AGU/Wiley, Frontiers) and institutional repositories (ICIMOD/HKH library, USGS, World Bank, UNDP) were searched using combinations of terms relating to Himalayan hazards, cascading and compound risk, glacial lake outburst floods, seismicity, permafrost and disaster risk reduction for literature published mainly between 2000 and 2026. Because this review draws on open-web-indexed academic search rather than paid bibliographic databases. It is presented as a structured systematic analysis; the eligibility screening, source list and limitations of this approach are stated explicitly in the Methods section. papers.title: Python and Stan code for Bayesian latent-regime analysis of delayed rainfall-induced landslides
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This software archive contains the Python and Stan source code used for the analyses reported in the Earth's Future manuscript “Latent infiltration regimes mediate environmental controls on delayed rainfall-induced landslides.” The software implements data preprocessing, environmental-control analyses, principal component analysis, soil-thickness and lag-time analyses, predictor–lag relationships, correlation and Mantel analyses, Bayesian latent-regime inference, WAIC-based model selection, posterior predictive checks, regime–soil-thickness analyses, Random Forest and XGBoost environmental attribution, SHAP analysis, and generation of the main and supplementary figures. The Bayesian latent-regime analysis is implemented using Stan and CmdStanPy. Candidate numbers of latent regimes are evaluated using WAIC, with the selected model subsequently used for posterior regime inference and environmental attribution. Version 1.0.0 corresponds to the software release associated with the manuscript submitted to Earth's Future. The software is openly developed at GitHub:https://github.com/liqi1919/Supporting-Materials

papers.title: Empirically informed AHP-FR modeling for multi-hazard susceptibility mapping in a mountainous transport corridors
papers.summary: Abstract Mountainous transport corridors are increasingly exposed to interacting natural hazards that intensify infrastructure, socio-economic, and land-use risks. However, most susceptibility assessments for high-mountain corridors still focus on single hazards or rely heavily on expert-based weighting, which can introduce subjectivity into spatial decision-making. This study develops an empirically informed Analytical Hierarchy Process–Frequency Ratio (AHP-FR) framework for integrated landslide, debris-flow, and flood susceptibility mapping along the Barakhan–Gilgit–Juglot section of the northern China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). The main methodological contribution is the use of frequency-ratio-derived empirical evidence that was integrated with AHP-derived factor weights to calculate final subclass weights and thereby reducing reliance on purely subjective expert judgment. Field surveys, remote sensing datasets, historical hazard inventories, and 12 conditioning factors were integrated in a GIS environment to generate single-hazard susceptibility maps and an eight-class multi-hazard susceptibility map. Independent ROC-AUC validation showed acceptable to very good predictive performance, with AUC values of 0.803 for landslides, 0.762 for debris flows, and 0.872 for floods. The results indicate that 63% of the corridor is exposed to one or more hazards, including 59% exposed to two or more overlapping hazards; 41% are co-susceptible to landslides and debris flows, while 37% falls within the no/very low multi-hazard susceptibility class. The spatial outputs identify major hazard-prone sections, including Attabad, Chalt, and Passu, providing practical guidance for road-maintenance prioritization, slope-stabilization planning, drainage improvement, and emergency preparedness. The added value of this study lies in combining empirical FR-based weighting with AHP and translating separate hazard maps into explicit multi-hazard combination classes, offering a repro

papers.title: Effects of mapping units on landslide susceptibility assessment: a comparative analysis of slope units and raster cells
papers.summary: The choice of spatial mapping units substantially shapes the accuracy, spatial detail, and interpretability of landslide susceptibility assessment (LSA). To investigate how mapping-unit selection affects LSA performance, this study used Hejing County, Xinjiang, China, as a case study. Based on a historical landslide inventory and a multi-source environmental-factor database, two mapping-unit schemes were constructed: 30 m raster cells and slope units extracted through a hydrology-based delineation method. Based on twelve selected conditioning factors, landslide susceptibility was modeled using four machine-learning algorithms, including logistic regression (LR), multilayer perceptron (MLP), random forest (RF), and XGBoost. In addition, the SHAP method was applied to examine differences in model decision mechanisms and factor contributions between the two mapping-unit schemes. The findings indicate that both mapping-unit schemes are capable of representing the spatial variability of LSA across the study area. The raster-cell-based scheme generally showed better predictive performance, with the mean AUC of the four models increasing from 0.798 under the slope-unit scheme to 0.859 under the raster-cell scheme. This indicates that raster cells are more effective in capturing localized environmental heterogeneity and small-scale high-susceptibility patches. In contrast, the slope-unit-based scheme reduced inter-model performance differences and generated more spatially continuous and stable susceptibility zonation consistent with natural slope boundaries. SHAP analysis further indicates that the dominant conditioning factors were generally consistent between the two schemes; however, raster-cell-based models were more sensitive to localized disturbances and micro-topographic variability, whereas slope-unit-based models emphasized the integrated constraints of geomorphological structure and hydrological processes. papers.title: Dynamic response and damage mechanism of deep overburden layer slope based on shaking table tests
papers.summary: The mountain areas of southwest China are widely covered with loose fractured rock bodies, which are prone to large-scale landslides under seismic action. It is known that the response of the acceleration amplification factor field is closely related to the seismic damage state of the overburden. In order to study the dynamic response and damage mechanism of overburden layer slopes under seismic action, a deep base-covered slope model containing two layers of stacks is used as a prototype in this study, and a series of shaking-table modeling experiments of progressive damage of earthquake-induced slopes are carried out. The cumulative seismic damage deformation process of the slope overburden was identified based on embedded sensors and Particle Image Velocimetry technology, and the energy transfer mechanism of the process was revealed by Hilbert Huang transform. The results show that the non-coherent motion (vibration frequency difference) between the shallow overburden layer-thick overburden layer-bedrock layer is the main controlling factor inducing the slope landslide, and the damage form of the deep overburden slope manifests itself in the form of the trailing edge sliding and extruding the central shear out. The damage starts from the back edge of the slope with increasing seismic intensity and gradually moves toward the middle to lower part of the slope, while extending from the surface to the deeper part of the slope.

papers.title: Explainable Machine Learning-Based Multi-Hazard Risk Assessment and Upazila-Level Intervention Prioritization in the Chattogram Region, Bangladesh
papers.summary: The increasing occurrence of natural hazards, either individually or in combination, has intensified disaster risk worldwide, with the Chattogram Region of Bangladesh representing a prominent multi-hazard hotspot where earthquakes, landslides, and floods frequently coexist. An interpretable GIS–ML-based multi-hazard risk assessment (MHRA) framework was developed to generate earthquake, landslide, and flood susceptibility zones (EQSZ, LSSZ, and FSZ) using ensemble machine learning algorithms, with model predictions explained through SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). The resulting susceptibility maps were integrated into a Multi-Hazard Index, which was then combined with a Vulnerability Index to produce the final Multi-Hazard Risk Zone (MHRZ). GBM achieved the highest predictive performance for earthquake (AUC = 0.799) and landslide (AUC = 0.786), whereas RF performed best for flood susceptibility (AUC = 0.917). SHAP identified shear-wave velocity (Vs30), Soil Moisture Index, and elevation as the most influential predictors of earthquake, landslide, and flood susceptibility, respectively. Although the eastern hill districts exhibited the highest multi-hazard susceptibility, the MHRZ identified the densely populated upazilas of Chattogram and Cox's Bazar as the highest-risk areas because socio-economic vulnerability outweighed comparatively moderate hazard susceptibility. Approximately 55.10% of the study area fell within the very low to low-risk classes, whereas only 21.49% fell within the high-to-very-high-risk classes, highlighting the critical role of socio-economic vulnerability in shaping regional disaster risk. The proposed MHRA framework offers a methodologically transferable basis for evidence-based disaster risk reduction (DRR) by enabling upazila-level policy screening, preliminary DRR intervention prioritization, and resilient spatial planning in multi-hazard, data-scarce regions.

papers.title: Analyzing Seismic and Acoustic Signals with Network-Based Coherence and Phase
papers.summary: Abstract The seismoacoustic wavefield contains a variety of signals that can be challenging to detect and characterize, particularly those that are weak, emergent, or visible only on a subset of stations. A few examples of such sources include volcanic and tectonic tremor, anthropogenic noise, landslides, and glaciers. Here, we present network-based coherence—a simple cross-spectral method applicable to both seismic and acoustic sensors in network or array configurations. The method enhances signals that are coherent across multiple stations while suppressing noise unique to individual sensors, enabling robust detection of subtle seismoacoustic sources. Building on this, we introduce a phase-based acoustic source localization method that uses interstation phase differences to locate non-impulsive signals. We demonstrate these methods on data from an operational volcano seismic network and an International Monitoring System infrasound array. At Mount Spurr, Alaska, seismic network coherence reveals weak, ephemeral tremor during a period of unrest in 2024–2025. At the infrasound array I53US, array coherence identifies monochromatic and frequency-gliding noise sources, and phase-based location attributes a persistent ∼2 Hz signal to a nearby power plant. We envision this approach as a tool for data quality control, volcano monitoring, and noise assessment across seismic or acoustic networks and arrays.

papers.title: Climate Change and Environmental Degradation: The 2023 Earthquake in Turkey and Syria
papers.summary: This chapter provides an in-depth analysis of the 2023 earthquake that struck Turkey and Syria, focusing on its seismological, humanitarian, socioeconomic, public health, and environmental impacts. It begins with an overview of the geographic and geological factors that underpin the region&s;s vulnerability to seismic activity. The chapter explores the earthquake&s;s magnitude, depth, tectonic features, aftershock activity, and comparisons with past seismic events in the region. A subsequent section discusses rapid response efforts by local and international organizations, the challenges faced by rescue teams, and the provision of medical and psychological support for survivors. The socioeconomic repercussions are analyzed, with emphasis on impacts on local economies, housing, and long-term developmental challenges posed by displacement. The chapter also addresses significant public health concerns, such as sanitation and mental health issues, that emerged in the aftermath. Finally, it examines the environmental toll, including changes to natural landscapes, landslides, soil liquefaction, and potential long-term ecological consequences. This concise chapter aims to offer insights into the complex interplay between natural disasters and human resilience in the face of catastrophic events.

papers.title: Automated Landslide Scar Detection in the Himalayan Region Using Satellite Imagery and YOLO-Based Deep Learning Models
papers.source: Journal of the Geological Society of India
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Landslides in the Himalayan region are the most serious hazards due to their destructive consequences in the context of life and the economy. More landslides are anticipated based on the present environmental and climatic scenario. Hence, a landslide information detection model is the foremost for hazard risk assessment. The application of deep learning algorithms in hazard analysis has gained significant attention worldwide. Moreover, remote sensing technology has emerged as a critical tool in diverse applications. Therefore, this study leverages the recent scientific and technological developments for extracting landslide-related information. We applied four YOLO (You Only Look Once) models, specifically YOLOv5, YOLOv6, YOLOv7, and YOLOv8, alongside eleven additional YOLO variants to detect landslide scars from satellite imagery. The study focuses on the Greater Himalayan Range, Nepal, utilising a dataset of 275 satellite images, divided into training, validation, and testing sets. The standard quantitative indicators, i.e., precision, recall, F-score, and mean average precision (mAP), are used for evaluation. The results indicate that YOLOv8 achieved the highest accuracy (F-score: 0.857), followed by YOLOv5, YOLOv7, and YOLOv6. These findings highlight the potential of YOLO-based models for rapid and accurate landslide detection, contributing to efficient hazard assessment and disaster response efforts.

papers.title: Voter Switching and Policy Preferences: Evidence from Japan's 2025–2026 Elections
papers.source: The Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance
papers.summary: This study examines vote switching between Japan’s July 2025 House of Councilors and February 2026 House of Representatives elections. The Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) suffered a major defeat in 2025 and then achieved a landslide victory in 2026 under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who adopted a moderate but firmly immigration-restrictive platform. Using a survey of 14,000 respondents and multinomial logit and probit models, we analyze party choice and vote switching. The major findings are as follows: (1) anti-consumption-tax attitudes are negatively associated with voting for the LDP and positively associated with voting for the right-wing Sanseito Party; (2) less opposition to foreigners as workplace colleagues relative to neighbors is positively associated with the probability of voting for the right-wing Sanseito Party; and (3) among voters for the right-wing Sanseito Party in 2025, less opposition to foreigners is positively associated with switching to the LDP in 2026.

papers.title: Comparative evaluation of frequency ratio and index of entropy models for landslides susceptibility mapping of Dikhow river basin, Northeast India
papers.summary: Landslide Susceptible Mapping is a significant approach in hilly regions for delineating the potential areas for landslide occurrence. North-eastern states of India are most prone to landslides due to intense monsoonal rainfall, complex geology, and increasing anthropogenic activities. A significant portion of the Dikhow River Basin lies within the hilly regions of Nagaland, where intense monsoonal rainfall and fragile geological conditions trigger slope instability. Numerous reported landslide incidents highlight the severity of this disaster in this region. This research focuses on the comparative assessment of two landslide susceptibility maps generated from two bivariate models, namely (i) Frequency Ratio (FR) and (ii) Index of Entropy (IOE), in the Dikhow River Basin by integrating 12 landslide triggering factors and 632 landslide inventories using Geospatial Technology. The generated Landslide Susceptibility Map has been categorized into five hierarchical classes, from very low to very high, using the natural-break classification system. The study indicated that 19.9% and 8.4% of the study area correspond to very high susceptibility to landslides by FR and IOE, respectively. The validation results illustrated satisfactory performance for both models with AUC values of 0.81 and 0.79 for the training datasets, and 0.82 and 0.8 for the testing datasets, respectively. R-index values indicate that 64.81% (FR) and 60.25% (IOE) of landslide occurrences were associated with very high susceptibility classes. The validation process reveals that the FR has better success in comparison to the IOE model. In order to reduce the negative effects of landslide hazards, the suggested research will assist government, policymakers, and decision-makers in managing and mitigating the adverse consequences of landslides.

When the mass of soil on a slope cannot ensure the balance of the forces acting on it, a landslide occurs, the area of the mass that is involved in the landslide is called a landslide body. When a slope landslide occurs, it is clear that there is a lack or weakening of the shear resistance of the sliding surface in order to maintain the equilibrium of the sliding body. The calculations of the safety factor are usually carried out according to the methods of limit equilibrium and the arcuate sliding surface. In the case of more complicated tasks (more complex, more complex conditions, the state of the rock mass and the size of the object) their solution by limit equilibrium methods is called into question. In such cases, numerical methods of calculation are also implemented, any of the methods for calculating the full state of stress and deformation of the given model. After that, the results obtained by the limit equilibrium methods are compared and the final conclusions are drawn by numerical methods.

papers.title: An Unsteady Seepage Calculation Method Based on an Improved Voronoi Pipe-Domain Mesh and ADE Finite Difference Scheme
papers.summary: Cracking of water diversion channel linings can induce localized unsteady seepage, and the resulting soil deformation process may seriously affect engineering safety. This paper proposes an unsteady seepage calculation method based on a Voronoi pipe-domain mesh and an ADE finite difference scheme. To address the limitation of the conventional pipe-domain method, in which boundary particles cannot be completely enclosed by the fluid computational domain, a Voronoi flow network construction method based on the relationships among adjacent particles is adopted to establish an irregular seepage spatial discretization model, providing a spatial basis for particle-scale seepage calculations. On this basis, to overcome the difficulty of directly applying the finite difference method to Voronoi irregular meshes, a local regular virtual grid is constructed, and a permeability coefficient-weighted interpolation method is employed to reconstruct pore-water pressures at virtual nodes, thereby establishing an unsteady seepage difference calculation method applicable to irregular meshes. Furthermore, an analytical hydraulic head field is used to evaluate the interpolation accuracy of virtual nodes, and the variation and convergence characteristics of interpolation errors under different mesh resolutions are analyzed. The stability condition of the difference scheme is derived based on Fourier analysis, and the relationships among the time step, spatial step, and permeability coefficient are clarified. The one-dimensional seepage validation in homogeneous soil demonstrates that the proposed method can reasonably describe the evolution of pore-water pressure, and the pore-water pressure exhibits an approximately linear relationship with the hydraulic gradient. Parameter analysis indicates that the time step, spatial step, and permeability coefficient jointly influence computational accuracy, stability, and efficiency. papers.title: Institutional Framework for Disaster Management in Karnataka
papers.summary: Disaster management has emerged as a critical dimension of public governance because climate change, environmental degradation, rapid urbanization and socio-economic vulnerability are increasing the frequency and consequences of disasters. Karnataka presents a particularly important case because of its multi-hazard profile, which includes recurrent droughts, floods, landslides, heat waves, cyclonic disturbances, urban flooding and other human-induced emergencies. This study examines the institutional framework for disaster management in Karnataka with particular reference to the Disaster Management Act, 2005, the Karnataka State Disaster Management Authority (KSDMA), State Executive Committee (SEC), District Disaster Management Authorities (DDMAs), Karnataka State Natural Disaster Monitoring Centre (KSNDMC), line departments and local governance institutions. The study adopts a qualitative documentary research design based on government policy documents, State and District Disaster Management Plans, KSDMA and KSNDMC documents, Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) reports, and contemporary academic literature published between 2021 and 2026. Particular attention is given to the 2018–2020 Kodagu landslides and the recurrent 2019–2022 floods in Belagavi and North Karnataka as case studies of institutional performance. The findings indicate that Karnataka has developed a comprehensive formal institutional architecture, but substantial implementation gaps remain in human resources, financial management, mitigation planning, early-warning infrastructure, inter-agency coordination, rehabilitation and local-level participation. The CAG’s 2025 performance audit provides evidence of significant vacancies in disaster response forces, delayed planning, under-utilisation of mitigation resources, deficiencies in hazard mapping and weaknesses in flood and landslide preparedness. The study argues that Karnataka’s principal challenge is not institutional absence but an implementati

Assessing agricultural drought intensification and spatiotemporal pattern in the central Rift Valley using multi-source indices
papers.summary: Drought is a complex and multifaceted phenomenon that includes meteorological, agricultural, hydrological, and socio-economic components. Both single and composite drought indices were used in this study to assess agricultural drought in the East Shewa Zone of Central Ethiopia. The Precipitation Condition Index (PCI), Temperature Condition Index (TCI), Vegetation Condition Index (VCI), and Soil Moisture Condition Index (SMCI) were used as single indices. To improve drought characterization, three composite indices—the Scaled Drought Condition Index (SDCI), Vegetation Health Index (VHI), and Optimized Vegetation Dryness Index (OVDI)—were created using empirical weighting and limited optimization techniques. The association of both single and composite indices with the multi-timescale Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), a widely used meteorological drought measure, was evaluated using in-sample correlation analysis. The results showed that the composite indices (OVDI, VHI, and SDCI) exhibited stronger associations with the multi-timescale SPI than the individual indices, although the strength of these associations varied across seasons and SPI timescales. Among the single indices, the PCI showed the strongest in-sample correlation with the short-term SPI ( r = 0.764 with SPI-1). In contrast, the VCI and SMCI were more strongly correlated with longer-term SPI scales, with SMCI showing in-sample correlations of ( r = 0.577 with SPI-3) and ( r = 0.467 with SPI-6). Spatiotemporal analysis indicated an increase in drought severity, with the area classified as severely dry expanding from 1% to 11% between 2002 and 2015. The findings provide insights into the use of remote sensing indices for drought monitoring and may contribute to the development of improved drought monitoring and early warning approaches in the region.

Calculations were performed for two reinforcement options: rock riprap and pile field (length 5 m, spacing 2.5 m). Results: the factor of safety for rock riprap was 2.53, and for the pile field — 2.41. Both values exceed regulatory requirements (1.15–1.30). The seasonal freezing depth in the region reaches 2.0–2.5 m. Practical significance: the results can be applied in the design of roads on sections of the Baikal- Amur Mainline. Effects of Herbaceous and Shrub Species on Soil Erosion Resistance and Root–Soil Reinforcement of Arid Slopes
papers.summary: Vegetation restoration can reduce soil erosion and improve soil stability on erosion-prone slopes, but the contrasting roles of herbaceous and shrub species in surface erosion resistance and subsurface reinforcement remain unclear. This study compared two herbaceous species, Melilotus officinalis (L.) Pall (MOP) and Suaeda glauca (Bunge) Bunge (SGB), and two shrub species, Alhagi camelorum Fisch. (ACF) and Nitraria tangutorum Bobrov (NTB), with bare soil (CK) as the control. Soil detachment capacity (Dc), root–soil shear strength, root traits, and soil properties were measured using planting experiments, flume scouring tests, and direct shear tests. Compared with CK, the vegetation treatments showed lower bulk density and higher total porosity and water-stable aggregates content, while soil organic matter exhibited differences among treatments. Herbaceous species developed dense fine roots in surface soil, whereas shrubs had deeper, coarser root systems. Vegetation significantly increased root–soil shear strength, mainly by increasing cohesion; herbs provided stronger surface reinforcement, whereas shrubs maintained more stable reinforcement at depth. All vegetation treatments significantly reduced Dc, and MOP showed the best overall anti-erosion performance. Random forest analysis further showed that root traits dominated Dc variation, accounting for 84.9% of total variable importance, with root length density and root surface area density as the leading factors. A regression model based on shear stress, total porosity, bulk density, and root length density predicted Dc well (R2 = 0.86, NSE = 0.65, RMSE = 0.083). These findings support site-specific vegetation selection: herbs for surface erosion control, shrubs for slope-stability concerns, and shrub–herb combinations where both risks coexist.

papers.title: Landfill Leachate Generation, Migration and Impacts on Soil and Groundwater Systems: A Review of Global, African and Nigerian Perspective
papers.source: IIARD INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF GEOGRAPHY AND ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT
papers.summary: Municipal solid waste generation is rising rapidly worldwide, and in many low- and middle income countries disposal remains dominated by open dumping without engineered containment, creating persistent conditions for the generation and uncontrolled migration of landfill leachate. This review synthesises global, African and Nigerian evidence on the composition, environmental behaviour and public health implications of landfill leachate, with particular attention to humid tropical and Niger Delta settings. Leachate composition is shown to evolve with waste age, climate and landfill design, shifting from organically dominated, high-BOD acidogenic-phase leachate towards ammonia- and chloride-dominated methanogenic-phase leachate over time. Once generated, contaminant transport is governed by the interaction of climate-driven infiltration, subsurface lithology and groundwater flow, conceptualised through the Source-Pathway-Receptor framework and explained mechanistically by Darcy's Law, Toth's groundwater flow system theory and the water balance concept. Empirical studies from Europe, North America, Asia, Africa and Nigeria consistently associate unlined dumpsites with elevated heavy metals, nutrients, organic loading and microbial contamination in soil and groundwater, with health consequences ranging from methemoglobinemia and gastrointestinal disease to chronic heavy-metal toxicity, alongside socio-economic impacts including declining property values and disproportionate exposure of low-income communities. Within the Niger Delta and Port Harcourt specifically, high rainfall, unconsolidated sandy aquifers and shallow groundwater tables create conditions of especially high intrinsic vulnerability. The review identifies persistent gaps in the integration of hydrogeophysical, geotechnical, hydrochemical and public health evidence within a single analytical framework, and in the treatment of seasonal variability, and argues that closing these gaps is essential for developi

papers.title: Heterogeneous soils – residual soils
papers.summary: Residual soils formed by physical and chemical weathering processes in situ are heterogeneous soils which vary spatially in properties and composition and vary from completely weathered rock to highly weathered rock. Extensive deposits are found in the tropics but these soils occur in all climatic zones. They can be difficult to sample and test, are partially saturated, have weak bonds, are highly permeable, and exhibit swelling, collapse and loss of strength when subject to changes in effective stress or water content. Properties of residual soils are affected by the test preparation process. Therefore, correlations developed for sedimentary soils may not apply to residual soils. Current properties are not related to stress history since the solids volume decreases as a result of weathering. They can show similar characteristics to overconsolidated soils when loaded but this is due to particle bonding, a result of partial saturation or chemical bonding. They can be in a metastable state which will collapse when sheared, stable-contractive state which causes small strains until yield point when significant straining occurs, or in stable-dilatant state when soil expands when sheared. Residual soil can exhibit fine-grained and coarse-grained behaviour. Collapse of partially saturated residual soils is prevented by controlling infiltration and groundwater. Rainfall induced slope failures are common in residual soils.

papers.title: Modelling soil-root interactions in partly saturated soils: a soil mechanics approach
papers.summary: Soil bioengineering using vegetation is a cost-effective and environmentally sustainable approach for soil stabilisation and enhancing the resilience of civil engineering earthworks. Plants provide hydrological reinforcement to the soil by regulating water content through the evapotranspiration process. Additionally, the presence of root biomass within the soil matrix enhances the soil’s shearing resistance through mechanical entanglement with the surrounding soil. Understanding the hydro-mechanical soil-root interactions is of paramount importance for safe and serviceable geotechnical infrastructure analysis and design. The first phase of this thesis (Chapter 3) focuses on the hydrological soil-root interactions and effects on it. A fully coupled mathematical model is developed to describe the interaction between precipitation, the growing plant root, and the physical properties of the underlying soil layer. A nondimensionalisation technique is used to reduce double-layered soil models to one-layer models by replacing the underlying soil layer with appropriate basal boundary conditions. This model is then used to simulate the spatiotemporal hydro-mechanical response of variably layered vegetated partly saturated soils. The outcomes indicate that root water uptake and porewater pressure interact significantly with the basal boundary condition. Results also suggest that plant roots prevent the development of high water pressures within shallow zones, confirming their importance in maintaining the safety and serviceability of earthwork slopes. The remaining work in this thesis (Chapter 4) focuses on mechanical soil-root interactions with a particular emphasis on the mechanical vulnerability analysis of growing plant roots subject to moisture-driven soil movements. A beam-spring interface model is proposed for the mobilisation of soil resistance and calibrated against pullout experimental data of roots. papers.title: Integrated Irrigation and Disease Management Strategies for Sustainable Wheat Production and Improved Plant Health and Grain Yield
papers.source: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development
papers.summary: Wheat production was expected to provide reliable grain quality and farmer income while using less water and facing climatic variability, soil degradation, disease development, and rising energy costs. This literature-based paper critically synthesized verified research on irrigation, plant disease management, irrigation–disease interactions, sustainability, digital agriculture, and the Pakistan/developing-economy context. It considered irrigation and plant health as related management areas rather than completely separate input decisions. The available evidence did not identify a universal irrigation technology or deficit percentage. Instead, it supported a context-specific approach that considered stored soil water and rainfall, protected important growth stages, managed canopy humidity and nitrogen, used resistant cultivars and clean seed, and applied surveillance, forecasting, and fungicides when justified. Global and China-focused studies reported that moderate deficit or optimized water-saving irrigation could improve water productivity, whereas severe water deficit commonly reduced yield. Jointing/stem elongation was repeatedly identified as an important stage for avoiding water stress, while anthesis and early grain filling were also important when water availability and disease risk required attention. Disease-management evidence emphasized genetic resistance, sanitation, crop rotation, scouting, and forecasting before chemical control. Fusarium head blight required particular attention to weather conditions around anthesis, residue inoculum, cultivar resistance, fungicide timing, and deoxynivalenol risk. Irrigation increased yield without increasing disease in some environments, although dense nitrogen-rich canopies, overhead wetting, and saturated soils could favor foliar diseases and waterlogging. papers.title: Impacts of Climate Variability on Infiltration and Groundwater Recharge in the Southeastern Coastal Region of Côte d'Ivoire
papers.summary: This study assesses the impacts of climate variability on infiltration and groundwater recharge within the southeastern coastal corridor of Côte d'Ivoire, spanning from Abidjan to Aboisso. The methodology integrates the Pettitt test to detect rainfall stationarity breaks, followed by water balance modeling using the Thornthwaite and Tixeront–Berkaloff methods to quantify infiltration. The analysis relies on a multi-decadal meteorological dataset, including a 54-year rainfall series (1960–2014) and a 43-year temperature record (1971–2014), coupled with a 23-year historical groundwater level monitoring dataset (1982–2005) obtained from deep boreholes. precipitation fluctuations were correlated with piezometric level variations across 30 shallow wells and 9 deep boreholes. The results identify a critical regional rainfall break occurring in 1982. Annual infiltration available for aquifer recharge ranged from 0 mm to maximum values of 856 mm, 998 mm, and 1011 mm at the Adiaké, Abidjan-Airport, and Bingerville synoptic stations, respectively. Prior to the 1982 break, mean infiltration rates (456 mm, 437 mm, and 378 mm, respectively) exceeded runoff (300 mm, 292 mm, and 285 mm), accounting for over 55% of the total rainfall surplus (infiltration + runoff). Post-1982, infiltration significantly decreased, dropping to between 20% and 40% of the surplus. Consequently, piezometric heads in deep aquifers (30 to 90 m depth) declined by 1.3 to 5.3 m, with borehole recharge occurring exclusively when the preceding year's rainfall exceeded 1,750 mm. In contrast, shallow wells (water table depth: 0.45 to 12.46 m) exhibited near-instantaneous recharge responses following rainfall events. Beyond quantifying volumetric variations, the scientific implications of these findings highlight a structural transition in the regional hydrological regime. papers.title: Contribution of soil coarse fragments to plant available water
papers.summary: Stony soils are widespread and used for food production, but the effect of coarse fragments (CFs) on water retention remains poorly understood. This study aimed to assess whether the available water (AW) retained in CFs depends on their size and porosity. CFs from three contrasting sites in southern Brazil, varying in size and porosity, were analyzed. Measurements included their volume, total porosity, bulk density, and water retention at suctions of 1 m and 150 m. AW was estimated as the difference of water retention between suctions of 1 m and 150 m. For each site, linear regression was used to evaluate the relationship of AW in CFs with total porosity, water-filled porosity at 1 m suction (θ 1m ), and volume of CFs. Results showed that AW in soil coarse fragments (CFs) depends almost exclusively on their porosity (R 2 around 0.99), while CF size has a negligible effect (R 2 ≤ 0.10). Compared to CFs total porosity, the CFs water-filled porosity at a suction of 1 m is a slightly better predictor of AW in CFs, but the total porosity of CFs is advantageous because its determination is less laborious and equipment-dependent. The relationship between AW and porosity in CFs depends on CFs parent rock lithology and weathering degree, which implies in calibration demands of a pedofunction type AW (porosity).

papers.title: A case study on SWMM based evaluation of rain barrel and downspout disconnection scenarios for urban stormwater management
papers.summary: Colombo, the executive and judicial capital of Sri Lanka, is located on the southwestern coast of the country and has experienced rapid urbanization in recent years, driven by infrastructure development, land use changes, and the growing impacts of climate change. These factors have significantly increased the frequency and severity of urban flooding. Therefore, this study explores the stormwater management problems in the 686.3-hectare study catchment, adjacent to the Kelani River in suburban Colombo, and proposes effective stormwater management strategies to avoid flooding in the area. Using GIS-based analysis, the study area was divided into 36 sub-catchments to determine the elevation and imperviousness characteristics of the study area and generate a Digital Elevation Model (DEM). Additionally, land use and land cover (LULC) mapping and change detection analysis were carried out using ArcGIS. The obtained spatial data were used in the EPA-SWMM model to evaluate stormwater responses under different rain barrel-based LID scenarios. Three scenarios were evaluated: the existing condition (no LID), rain barrel with downspout connection (No Disconnect), and rain barrel with downspout disconnection (Disconnect). The runoff coefficients for the baseline scenario were 0.849 and 0.871 for the 2-year and 10-year storms, respectively. The rain barrel with-disconnect scenario reduced these to 0.379 and 0.456, while the no-disconnect scenario resulted in 0.563 and 0.598, respectively. The Disconnect configuration proved most effective in reducing average total runoff by 55% and 48% for the 2-year and 10-year storms, respectively, while more than doubling infiltration rates. In contrast, the No Disconnect configuration provided only moderate runoff reduction through temporary storage, without meaningfully restoring natural infiltration processes. Moreover, Outfall loading was 196.15 and 234.28 L under existing conditions for the 2- and 10-year storms, respectively. The discon

papers.title: Towards Sustainable Mine Restoration: Environmental Safety Assessment of Phosphorus Migration Following Sewage Sludge Compost Application to Abandoned Phosphate Mines in Southwestern China
papers.summary: Repurposing waste-derived organic amendments for degraded land restoration supports the transition toward a circular economy, yet the associated environmental risks must be rigorously evaluated to ensure long-term sustainability. Sewage sludge compost (SSC) is a promising soil amendment for the ecological restoration of abandoned phosphate-mine sites (APMSs). However, SSC application may alter phosphorus (P) migration and release, thereby posing a risk of secondary pollution that could undermine the sustainability of mine reclamation efforts. Here, dynamic leaching-column experiments simulating three years of natural rainfall infiltration were conducted to investigate P-release characteristics under different fertilization scenarios, including application rate, application method, and compost maturity. Ecological risk was evaluated using a modified phosphorus pollution index (PPI), and the likely mechanisms governing P leaching and release in APMS soils were explored. Dissolved reactive P was the predominant released form in all treatments, accounting for 67.9–85.6% of total released P. Increasing the SSC application rate reduced the cumulative total phosphorus (TP) release ratio (on a soil TP content basis) from 0.0348% in the unfertilized control to 0.0264–0.0299%. Deep full-profile incorporation within the upper 20 cm of APMS soil and subsurface application reduced TP release by 36.8% and 34.1%, respectively, relative to shallow full-profile incorporation within the upper 10 cm of APMS soil. Primary sewage sludge compost (SSC*) controlled P release only when cumulative rainfall infiltration was ≤669 mm; by the third year, the ecological risk increased from slight to the severe-pollution level. SSC applied at 120 t ha−1 under the shallow full-profile fertilization mode reduced the PPI of APMS1 and APMS2 by 30.8–44.8% and 5.6–12.3%, respectively. P dissolution was positively associated with Ca release. Humic substances likely formed larger, less mobile, non-rigid c

papers.title: The Effect of Climate Change and Land Use Change Scenarios on the Design Flood Discharge and the Curve Number: The Case of the Noelmina and Benanain Watersheds, Indonesia
papers.summary: Climate change substantially alters watershed hydrology, primarily through increased flood discharge. This study uses the Hydrologic Engineering Center’s Hydrologic Modeling System (HEC-HMS) to assess how climate change and land-use change scenarios affect the design flood discharge and Curve Number (CN) for the Noelmina and Benanain watersheds in East Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia. The Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) 2.6 and 8.5 were applied for the periods 2041-2060 and 2081-2100. The simulated flood discharge increased progressively over time, most notably under the high-emission RCP 8.5 scenario towards the end of the century. Compared with the discharge from observed rainfall in 2024, the 25-year design flood under RCP 8.5 (2081-2100) increased by 35.6% in Noelmina and 32.6% in Benanain, while the 50-year flood increased by 36.3% and 30.7%, respectively. A land-use analysis conducted between 2015 and 2024 revealed the conversion of vegetated land into residential and agricultural areas. This raised the composite CN from 83.19 to 83.73 in Noelmina and from 85.99 to 86.82 in Benanain. This indicates a reduction in infiltration capacity and an increase in surface runoff. The combined effects of climate change and land use are likely to exacerbate future flood risk, highlighting the need for integrated watershed management and adaptive mitigation strategies.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence applications in porous asphalt pavement
papers.source: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
papers.summary: Porous asphalt pavement (PAP) was developed as a sustainable pavement solution to improve rainwater infiltration, reduce inundation, and improve driving safety. The performance of PAP is influenced by the complex interactions between pore structures, clogging mechanisms, and structural and thermal responses, thus encouraging the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in its modeling. This study aims to comprehensively synthesize the application of AI in PAP through the systematic literature review (SLR) approach. The SLR process was carried out against the publication of the 2021–2026 period from the Elsevier, SpringerLink, and MDPI databases, which resulted in 10 high-quality articles for analysis. The results show that AI enables accurate and non-destructive prediction of hydraulic and clogging performance, while AI-integrated mechanistic models achieve a correlation coefficient of up to 0.994 for structural response and an error below 5% for thermal conductivity. Image-based deep learning and generative models further demonstrate potential for pavement condition assessment and porous microstructure modeling. The novelty of this review lies in integrating evidence on AI applications across the hydraulic, clogging, structural, thermal, and microstructural domains of PAP. The findings highlight the need for an integrated, material-specific AI framework to support sustainable PAP design, monitoring, and maintenance.

Flood Risk Assessment in Urban Environments: Dynamic Modeling and Multi-Scenario Analysis
papers.source: Journal of Geology Geography and Geoecology
papers.summary: Urban flooding has become one of the most significant challenges for rapidly urbanizing cities, where intensive land development, increasing impervious surfaces, and complex topography substantially amplify surface runoff and flash flood hazards. The aim of this study is to develop an integrated methodological framework for assessing urban flood risk through dynamic hydrological modelling and multi-scenario spatial analysis using Geographic Information Systems. The study was conducted within a highly urbanized micro-catchment located in the Yasamal district of Baku, Azerbaijan, characterized by steep relief, predominantly impermeable clay soils, and dense urban development. The methodology combines Digital Elevation Model analysis, land use and land cover assessment, hydrological soil classification, the Rational and Soil Conservation Service Curve Number methods, runoff concentration modelling based on the National Resources Conservation Service Kinematic Wave approach, and Geographic Information Systems-based spatial analysis. Rainfall scenarios ranging from 1 to 100 mm were simulated to evaluate runoff generation, peak discharge, flood propagation, and the spatial distribution of flood hazards at the individual building level. The results demonstrate that the interaction between relief morphology, intensive urbanization, and low soil infiltration capacity creates favourable conditions for rapid stormwater accumulation and flash flood formation. Approximately 79% of the total runoff is concentrated within three critical topographic depressions, while floodwaters reach the most vulnerable buildings within only 3.0–4.3 minutes under high-intensity rainfall scenarios. Comparative analysis revealed that the Rational method provides more reliable estimates of peak discharge and runoff concentration time, whereas the Soil Conservation Service Curve Number method more accurately predicts runoff volume. Useful for looking at the modelled water balance at one place at a time and for presentations. It yields no table or downloadable figures.

papers.title: A well-balanced local radial basis functions collocation method for single-layer and two-layer shallow water flows with rainfall and infiltration
Deep soil desiccation patterns and ecohydrological feedbacks of vegetation re-establishment in desiccated soils on the Loess Plateau
papers.summary: Deep soil water (>200 cm) is a critical water source for sustaining vegetation productivity and long term ecosystem stability in water limited regions. However, under the large scale “Grain for Green” program on the Loess Plateau, deep soil water patterns across different vegetation restoration types remain insufficiently understood. The ecohydrological feedbacks associated with vegetation reestablishment in desiccated soils are also unclear. This study integrated 6,516 observations from 176 sites across the Loess Plateau. We systematically assessed soil water conditions and desiccation characteristics within 0–1000 cm soil profiles under rainfed cropland, natural grassland, artificial grassland, orchards, and ecological forests (including tree and shrub plantations). In addition, a 5-year replanting experiment was conducted on soils with pre-existing deep desiccation (>10 m). The experiment compared the coupled responses of soil water dynamics and plant growth under different vegetation configurations. The results show that deep soil desiccation is widespread during vegetation restoration on the Loess Plateau. Rainfed orchards, ecological forests, and artificial grasslands developed persistent dry layers 3–5 m thick. The most severe desiccation occurred in ecological forests. Following replanting on desiccated soils, deep rooted species ( Robinia pseudoacacia L., Caragana korshinskii Kom., and Medicago sativa L.) continuously depleted middle and deep soil water because of their high water consumption. They also preferentially utilized infiltrated rainfall, thereby limiting deep recharge and maintaining or exacerbating soil desiccation. Meanwhile, these species exhibited a rainfall-pulse-driven adaptive growth strategy that supported survival and biomass accumulation. In contrast, shallow rooted vegetation ( Poa annua L.) and bare land showed limited utilization of deep soil water. Their low water consumption facilitated downward rainfall infiltration. papers.title: Porous Media Free-Flow Coupling - From REV to Pore Scale and Back
papers.summary: Flow and transport processes in domains composed of a porous medium and an adjacent free-flow region appear in a wide range of industrial, bio-medical and environmental applications. Industrial applications range from flow in fuel cells to drying processes; possible bio-medical applications include the interplay of distribution processes in blood vessels and in the surrounding tissue. Applications in environmental systems include infiltration of overland flow during rainfall, groundwater contamination due to infiltrating pollutants and evaporation from soil. One of the key challenges for coupled free flow and porous-medium flow arises from the fact that the overall effective behaviour depends strongly on interface processes that occur on small spatial scales (pore scale), although the overall system of interest is often too large to resolve these processes explicitly in detail. REV-scale models are usually not able to capture all the relevant physical processes for such coupled systems. For the accurate description of interface phenomena, it is therefore necessary to develop model concepts that combine information gained through pore-scale and REV-scale models. The first part of the lecture includes the following items: -an explanation of relevant processes of mass, momentum and energy transfer at the interface between a free-flow and a porous-media system; -a presentation of conceptual models for coupled single-phase free flow and two-phase porous-medium flow with a detailed description of the models in the free flow and in the porous medium for the pore and REV scale; -comparison studies to show the advantages and disadvantages in relation to classical approaches; the coupling concepts are discussed on the basis of different technical or environmental issues. In the second part of the lecture I would very much like to discuss the results on the basis of various detailed use cases.
