papers.title: Assessing the hydrological water balance of the poorly gauged semi-arid Oued Cherraa basin in northeastern Morocco using the SWAT model
papers.summary: Water resources management in semi-arid areas is facing increasing difficulties, which include climatic variability, excessive use of groundwater resources, and poor hydrometeorological network coverage, over-extraction of groundwater resources, and poor hydrometeorological network coverage. The main objective of this research is to apply the SWAT Water Budget module in estimating the hydrological water balance of the poorly gauged basin of Oued Cherraa in the Moulouya watershed in northeastern Morocco. It aims at quantifying the main components of the water balance: precipitation, evapotranspiration (ET), surface runoff, and groundwater recharge, on the one hand. On the other one, it is about analyzing their spatial variability in a data-scarce context. The SWAT model was implemented using available climatic data and daily discharge data from one hydrometric station called Tazarhine. The model was calibrated and validated using the SUFI-2 algorithm within the SWAT-CUP interface. The accuracy of the model simulation was considered to be acceptable due to the efficiency values of Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency being 0.58 and 0.60 for calibration and validation, respectively, as well as the percentage bias being minimal at − 9.1% and − 0.2%, also for calibration and validation, respectively. Moreover, sensitivity analysis indicated that the most influential parameters to the simulations are RCHRG_DP, ALPHA_BF and CN2. From water balance analysis, evapotranspiration is estimated to be responsible for almost 89% of precipitation, while surface runoff is less than 6%. Recharge of shallow aquifers is much more significant compared to recharge of deep aquifers, while irrigated areas demonstrate groundwater depletion. It is evident from these results that groundwater resources available in semi-arid areas where there is no adequate monitoring system are quite fragile, which proves the importance of SWAT as a decision-support tool.

papers.title: Friction over gravitational forcing: Disentangling the controls of Hortonian overland flow and erosion through energy-centred process modelling
papers.summary: Abstract. This study investigates the coupled dynamics of Hortonian overland flow (HOF) and sediment transport observed during rainfall simulations at the plot scale using the process-based Catflow model with an energy centred approach. A hierarchical calibration strategy was applied to reproduce overland flow generation, flow velocities in sheet and rill domains and sediment detachment sequentially, allowing the dominant controls on HOF and erosion processes to be identified. The results show that antecedent soil moisture and surface roughness are the primary controls on HOF generation, whereas rainfall intensity and slope had no significant effect within the investigated range. Increasing surface roughness reduced surface runoff and total sediment export, while simultaneously increasing the ratio between rill and sheet flow velocities, indicating enhanced flow concentration into preferential pathways. No clear relationship was observed between flow velocities and slope, demonstrating that overland flow dynamics are primarily limited by friction rather than gravitational forcing. The model reproduced overland flow generation, flow partitioning and total eroded sediment with good consistency. The results indicate that sheet flow primarily governs sediment detachment and energy dissipation, whereas rills function as efficient sediment transport pathways. Increasing surface roughness promoted flow concentration into rills, where the greater hydraulic radius reduced relative frictional losses and enabled a more efficient conversion of potential into kinetic energy. Consequently, downslope kinetic energy transport became increasingly dominant within the rill domain, while the overall system remained friction dominated. This energetic interpretation links overland flow generation, flow organisation and erosion dynamics through the balance between energy input, dissipation and redistribution. Overall, the study highlights the importance of frictional resistance as prime l

papers.title: The influence of playing surface quality and centralized venue transitions on match performance and non-contact injury incidence in the ethiopian premier league
Revisión de medidas para la mitigación de inundaciones implementando sistemas urbanos de drenaje sostenible y obras grises
papers.summary: The rapid increase in soil impermeability due to urban expansion, coupled with growing rainfall, causes flooding that affects residential homes, university campuses, and municipalities. Urban growth outpaces conventional storm drainage systems, which were designed with limited capacity, restricting infiltration and aquifer recharge, leading to increased surface runoff and high flood risks. This review synthesizes the implementation of Sustainable Urban Drainage Systems (SuDS) and grey infrastructure as a comprehensive approach. Flood scenarios and environmental issues in Latin America and worldwide were analyzed, proposing selection criteria with advantages and disadvantages for both measures. Additionally, key co-benefits related to health, human well-being, water quality improvement, environmental care, and enhanced urban landscaping are discussed. Finally, a guiding matrix was created summarizing the essential applicability of each type of SuDS and grey infrastructure, serving as a decision-making tool for urban planning, educational institutions, and engineering in general.

papers.title: Influence of Geogrid-Geotextile Reinforcement on Field-Derived Soil-Water Characteristic Curves and Climate-Driven Moisture Dynamics of Compacted Clay Slopes
papers.summary: Geosynthetic reinforcement is widely used to improve slope stability; however, its association with soil–water characteristic curve (SWCC) behavior under natural climatic exposure remains insufficiently understood. This study compared two geometrically identical outdoor reduced-scale compacted-clay slope models: one containing three geogrid-integrated geotextile layers and one unreinforced control. Sensors at a depth of 0.46 m recorded volumetric water content (VWC) and matric suction at 15-min intervals. Drying-path van Genuchten curves were evaluated over the common reliable suction domain of 5.0–51.1 kPa using a trailing 24-h classification and 2000 paired calendar-day bootstrap resamples. The reinforced curve remained above the control curve throughout this domain. The median reinforced-minus-control VWC difference decreased from 0.0454 m3/m3 at 5 kPa (95% conditional interval: 0.0351–0.0590) to 0.0126 m3/m3 at 51.1 kPa (0.0074–0.0180). This difference persisted across 182 sensitivity configurations, although individual model parameters were weakly identifiable. Across 21 rainfall events of at least 5 mm, the reinforced model exhibited smaller median VWC increases and suction decreases. These results provide quantitative benchmarks for interpreting and modeling hydraulic responses in reinforced clay systems. Because only one model represented each configuration and mechanical performance was not measured, the findings are conditional and do not establish a replicated reinforcement effect or improved slope stability.

papers.title: Wetting-history-dependent mechanical damage of unsaturated floodplain subgrade soil: strength-stiffness degradation and a unified piecewise constitutive model
Land-use controls on soil hydraulic functioning: the role of pore organization and gravel distribution in an agricultural catchment
papers.summary: Soil hydraulic functioning in headwater catchments reflects interactions among pore organization, land use, and coarse-fragment distribution, but the relative importance of these controls remains uncertain when point measurements are interpreted at broader spatial scales. This study evaluated how near-surface soil permeability and water storage varied among land-use and tillage systems and whether those variations were associated with soil structure and gravel distribution in a 1.19 km 2 agricultural headwater catchment in southern Brazil. Physical and hydraulic properties were measured in the 0–0.05 m layer at 69 sampling points (414 undisturbed cores), including bulk density, pore-size distribution, saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ksat), air permeability (Ka), water retention across matric potentials, gravel content, texture, and soil organic carbon (SOC). Planned contrasts, Pearson correlations, and principal component analysis (PCA) were used to evaluate group differences and multivariate associations. Natural forest had lower bulk density and greater permeability-related attributes than grazed grassland, whereas conservation tillage increased water retention and plant-available water relative to conventional tillage without a consistent increase in Ksat. Gravel abundance was positively associated with macroporosity, Ka, and Ksat and negatively associated with water retention near field capacity, but these correlations do not establish a causal pathway. Land-use differences in water retention were strongest near saturation and diminished at higher suctions. The first two PCA axes explained 49.3% of total variance and separated transmission-related attributes (Ksat, Ka, macroporosity, total porosity, and saturated water content) from denser, storage-related conditions, while substantial variability remained in higher components. papers.title: Soil Cracking in Vertisols: Mechanism, Impacts and Management Strategies
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Black cotton soil (Vertisols) exhibit pronounced surface cracking due to their high content of smectite‐rich clay minerals, which experiences intense shrink‐swell cycles during alternating wetting and drying conditions. These dynamic structural changes lead to the formation of deep and interconnected cracks, significantly influencing the soil structure, water infiltration, runoff generation, soil loss and overall soil stability. Consequently, the adoption of different sustainable soil and water management practices that regulate soil moisture regimes which is essential for minimizing surface cracking and enhancing the resilience of Vertisols under variable rainfall conditions. The results revealed that these management practices substantially reduced key cracking parameters, i.e., crack depth, width, length, area and volume ranging from 3.60%–40.6%, 3.80%–46.2%, 4.40%–41.4%, 5.80%–57.0% and 18.0%–74.0%, respectively. In addition to their effects on surface cracking, agronomic, biological and soil structural management practices resulted in marked reductions in runoff (3.30%–98.3%; 1.31–39.0 mm) and soil loss (2.30%–99.7%; 0.23–9.80 t ha −1 ) while enhancing water‐use efficiency (WUE) by up to 22.1%. Similarly, hydrological and land‐configuration practices, including broad‐bed and furrow systems, ridge‐furrow configurations, bunding and farm ponds reduced runoff by 6.44%–75.5% (1.65–26.8 mm), soil loss by 10.9%–98.0% (0.063–9.60 t ha −1 ) and improved WUE by 3.40%–41.5%. Inclusively, this review elucidates the mechanisms governing cracking behaviour in Vertisols and underscores the critical role of soil and water management practices in mitigating surface cracking, reducing runoff and soil loss and sustaining soil health. Therefore, the adoption of these practices is therefore vital for enhancing crop productivity and long‐term land resilience in semiarid and arid regions.

papers.title: Evolution Process and Failure Mechanism of a Multi‐Factor Coupled Loess Landslide: A Case Study in Xiangning County, China
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Loess landslides are major geohazards on the Chinese Loess Plateau, where rainfall and engineering activities commonly trigger slope failures that also drive slope‐to‐gully evolution. This study investigates the ZQ landslide (23 April 2023) in Xiangning County, Shanxi Province, using field surveys, UAV photogrammetry, SBAS‐InSAR, dynamic triaxial tests and finite‐element simulations to clarify deformation, material behaviour, geomorphic evolution and failure mechanisms. The landslide (200 m long, 308 m wide; 6.0 × 10 4 m 2 ) developed in a Quaternary loess–palaeosol sequence and showed episodic retrogression, producing three rear scarps. The sliding mass moved from one side of the gully toward the valley bottom, where the deposit partially occupied the gully and induced frontal bulging, showing local adjustment of the gully. SBAS‐InSAR revealed central displacement accumulation with peak line‐of‐sight displacement of −43.3 mm and a mean rate of −41 mm/year; deformation acceleration coincided with rainfall, especially the 71.6 mm total in April 2023. Dynamic triaxial tests show that saturated loess is sensitive to cyclic loading. Higher CSR and loading frequency accelerated plastic‐strain accumulation and dynamic strength degradation, providing laboratory evidence for cyclic‐load–induced weakening. Scenario‐based finite‐element modelling indicated progressive weakening under sustained rainfall. Under the coupled rainfall–vibration scenario, deformation became more toe‐controlled, with a maximum horizontal displacement of 4.28 m, toe uplift of 4.10 m and a factor of safety of 0.773. The development of a connected plastic zone indicates progressive failure and potential reactivation. The results suggest that rainfall‐driven infiltration softening within the loess–palaeosol stratigraphic structure was the main hydrological trigger, whereas mining‐related disturbance may have contributed to failure by promoting crack development, deformation accumulation and cyc

papers.title: Analisis Risiko Bencana Kekeringan Menggunakan Metode Kerawanan (Hazard), Kerentanan (Vulnerability) Dan Kapasitas (Capacity) Di Kelurahan Cilembang Kota Tasikmalaya
papers.summary: Drought is a hydrometeorological disaster that can threaten water availability and increase the vulnerability of urban communities. This study aims to analyze drought disaster risk in Cilembang Village, Tasikmalaya City, based on hazard, vulnerability, and capacity components. A descriptive approach combined with spatial analysis based on secondary data was employed. Hazard was assessed using rainfall, slope, soil type, geological structure, and land-use parameters; vulnerability covered economic, social, and environmental dimensions; while capacity was evaluated based on community and institutional preparedness. Each parameter was classified and scored, and the components were subsequently integrated through an overlay technique using ArcGIS 10.8. The results indicate that Cilembang Village has high drought hazard and vulnerability levels, influenced by low rainfall according to the classification applied in this study, the dominance of residential land use of approximately 90%, high population density, and limited water infiltration areas. Institutional capacity is already present; however, drought-specific early warning systems and community participation still require strengthening. The integration of hazard, vulnerability, and capacity indicates that Cilembang Village is classified as having a high drought risk. These findings emphasize the importance of water conservation, sustainable land-use management, and strengthening community capacity as key components of drought risk reduction strategies.

papers.title: Cloud computing and global satellite products for potential groundwater recharge estimation: application to the Basin of Mexico
papers.summary: Groundwater recharge (GWr) estimation is fundamental for assessing aquifer storage changes, ensuring groundwater sustainability, and supporting effective water management. However, regional groundwater recharge assessment remains challenging because it requires integrating large geospatial datasets, computational resources, and hydrogeological information that are often unavailable in data-limited regions. This study presents a cloud-based framework for estimating potential groundwater recharge (GWpr) using open satellite products and the Thornthwaite-Mather (T-M) water balance model implemented in Google Earth Engine (GEE) and executed through Google Colab. The framework integrates globally available datasets, including CHIRPS precipitation, MODIS potential evapotranspiration, and OpenLandMap soil properties, within a reproducible Python workflow that minimizes dependence on local computational infrastructure. The Basin of Mexico (BM), an endorheic volcanic basin affected by intensive groundwater exploitation, was selected as a case study to evaluate the framework against a previously calibrated Soil Water Balance (SWB) model. The proposed implementation estimated a mean annual ground water potential recharge (GWpr) of ~ 44.7 mm/year, closely matching the reference model at the basin scale. Differences between both approaches were ~ 4–5% in the Zona Metropolitana and Tecocomulco groundwater management units (GMUs), whereas larger discrepancies (~ 20–30%) occurred in eastern and northern GMUs, reflecting differences in model temporal representation and local hydroclimatic conditions. Overall, the proposed cloud-computing framework provides an accessible, reproducible, and transferable approach for estimating GWpr using globally available datasets, facilitating groundwater assessments in data-limited regions with diverse hydrogeological settings.

papers.title: Mass‐Conserving LSTM With Dual States for Streamflow Prediction: Separating Quickflow and Slow Storage
papers.source: Journal of Geophysical Research Machine Learning and Computation
papers.summary: Abstract We introduce a Mass‐Conserving Long Short‐Term Memory with Dual States (MC‐LSTM‐DS) with the intention of separating short‐ and long‐term memory for predicting streamflow. It enforces water balance through a new partition gate on precipitation. We benchmark MC‐LSTM‐DS against a standard Long Short‐Term Memory (LSTM) and the original Mass‐Conserving Long Short‐Term Memory (MC‐LSTM) on CAMELS‐IND for 158 basins. Skill score analysis of the three models reveals that enforcing mass conservation degrades performance in the semi‐arid and tropical monsoon regions. However, the addition of another cell state in MC‐LSTM‐DS improves performance over MC‐LSTM in these regions. The decomposition of model predictions suggests that the added long cell‐state captures slow storage and releases in the model, while the original state tracks quickflow. Their relative contributions vary systematically with climate, providing a hydrological representation of the cell states. The newly introduced partition mechanism captures signatures of different runoff‐generating processes. A basin‐scale water‐balance check suggests additional effective inflows in some monsoon‐dominated regions. This highlights the catchments where data or missing process representations (e.g., groundwater) may limit strict closure. We also evaluated our model's cross‐regional robustness on the CAMELS‐US data set across 531 basins. The performance of MC‐LSTM‐DS on the CAMELS‐US matches that of LSTM and MC‐LSTM in Nash‐Sutcliffe Efficiency and attains state‐of‐the‐art Kling‐Gupta Efficiency and FHV (High Flow Bias). This indicates its potential generalization across regions. This study establishes a binational benchmark and provides an interpretable, mass‐conserving deep learning framework for operational streamflow prediction across diverse hydroclimates.

papers.title: Integrated Remote Sensing And Gis-Based Mapping Of Groundwater Recharge Potential In The Velu River Basin, Maharashtra
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Abstract Groundwater recharge assessment is a critical component in ensuring water sustainability, particularly in hard rock and semi-arid regions where natural infiltration is limited. This study presents a GIS-based AHP framework specifically applied to semi-arid basaltic terrain integrating the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) with Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to delineate groundwater recharge potential zones (GWRPZ) in the Velu River basin, Pune district, Maharashtra, India. The approach uniquely combines thematic layers including land use/land cover, slope, geology, geomorphology, soil, rainfall, drainage, and lineament density, with weights assigned based on expert judgment, literature review, and field validation. The results classify the basin into five recharge zones, where 4.09% of the area has excellent recharge potential, while 45.02%, 43.80%, 5.99%, and 1.11% fall under good, moderate, poor, and very poor zones respectively. Model validation using Receiver Operating Characteristics (ROC) curve and Area Under Curve (AUC) yielded an accuracy of 84.4%, confirming the robustness of the methodology. The novelty of this research lies in its integrated, multi-criteria, GIS-based modelling approach, specifically developed and validated for complex semi-arid basaltic regions, which are under immense water stress. This study not only provides a high-resolution map of potential recharge zones but also offers a replicable and scientifically defensible tool for the spatial planning of water conservation structures and artificial recharge interventions. The resultant GWRPZ map and the underlying methodology are directly applicable to water resource managers, planners, and policy designers, serving as an essential input for crafting effective and sustainable groundwater development and management policies in the Velu River basin and similar climatic and geological settings across the Deccan Volcanic Province.

papers.title: Assessing the vulnerability of the Karaj aquifer with the upgraded Fuzzy DRASTIC+ model by combining water quality and land use indicators
Geotechnical Design and Construction of Gabion Shoreline Protection for an Integrated Creek Improvement Project in Diobu Creek, Port Harcourt, Niger Delta, Nigeria
papers.source: Journal of Civil Construction and Environmental Engineering
papers.summary: Urban waterways in the Niger Delta are increasingly exposed to channel siltation, bank erosion, uncontrolled waste deposition, hydraulic scour and progressive loss of channel capacity. These problems are particularly critical where shoreline stabilization must be undertaken concurrently with dredging, reclamation and navigation improvement on weak, saturated sediments. This study presents the geotechnical investigation, design and construction of a gabion-based shoreline protection system implemented as a component of the integrated improvement of Diobu Creek, Port Harcourt, Nigeria. The study combines topographic and bathymetric surveys, tidal observations, three geotechnical boreholes, particle-size analysis, permeability estimation and direct shear testing to establish the engineering conditions controlling shoreline stability and revetment performance. The investigated riverbed comprises approximately 1.2–1.6 m of very soft to soft organic silty clay underlain by predominantly medium-grained, relatively uniform sand extending to at least 12 m below the riverbed. The sand exhibits an estimated hydraulic conductivity of approximately (4.41 × 10 -3 ) m/s and an average angle of internal friction of about 34°. These conditions necessitated careful management of saturated sediments during excavation and construction below Low Low Water (LLW). The adopted protection system comprised shoreline sand filling and regrading, excavation of weak foundation sediments, placement of a 0.45 m crushed-stone foundation layer, installation of a high-strength geotextile filter/separator, placement and interconnection of zinc-coated gabion baskets filled with durable crushed rock, and construction of a crest/anchor beam. A 1V:2.5H bank slope was adopted to reduce the potential for instability while providing an appropriate geometry for the gabion revetment. Construction experience demonstrated that the principal geotechnical challenges were instability of saturated soft sediments, lo

papers.title: Quantification of hysteresis area and artificial intelligence-assisted prediction of cracking in biochar-amended soil under wet-dry cycles
papers.summary: This study investigates the coupled hysteresis-cracking interaction in expansive soil under wet-dry cycles, integrating artificial intelligence predictive modeling. Based on the Van Genuchten ( VG ) model, an analytical formula for hysteresis area and a one-dimensional crack depth equation considering hysteresis were developed. Laboratory experiments on expansive soil with varying biochar contents revealed hysteresis and crack patterns. Biochar optimizes soil structure via a bimodal pore system, reducing hysteresis and cracking. After 10 cycles, hysteresis area decreased by 37% in bare soil and 70% in 15% biochar-amended soil; the crack intensity factor after five cycles was 9.11 versus 15.17 for the control, confirming crack suppression. The analytical formula matched experimental data well ( R 2 > 0.98). Parameter sensitivity shows hysteresis area depends primarily on VG parameters α , n, and cycle number; higher α and n reduce hysteresis, and area stabilizes with increasing cycles. Hysteresis area strongly correlates with crack depth, serving as a cracking predictor. A mechanism-constrained random forest surrogate model ( R 2 = 0.93, RMSE = 0.82) was developed for rapid crack depth assessment under various material compositions and cycling conditions. These findings offer a theoretical foundation and data-driven techniques for screening protective materials and evaluating damage evolution in unsaturated soils under wet-dry cycling.

papers.title: Quantitative study on heat accumulation effect of large-scale water-conducting faults in faulted basins: A case study of the karst geothermal system in Xiongan New Area, Northern China
Sustainable Design of Closed Drainage Infrastructure for Flood Control in Manggala Makassar City, Indonesia
papers.source: Journal of Geoscience Engineering Environment and Technology
papers.summary: Manggala District in eastern Makassar City experiences recurrent urban flooding driven by rapid land-use conversion, undulating topography, and drainage channels whose hydraulic capacity has been degraded by sedimentation and waste. Previous studies in Makassar have largely evaluated open eco-drainage measures, infiltration wells, and retention ponds, but few have provided a reproducible, discharge-based design of a fully closed circular conduit network sized against a defined return period. This study addresses that gap by coupling frequency-based hydrological analysis with hydraulic design of a closed circular drainage system for the Zone 1 catchment of Manggala. Annual maximum daily rainfall from the Makassar station (2014–2024) was fitted to candidate distributions and evaluated with goodness-of-fit tests; the 10-year design storm was propagated to peak discharge using the rational method with land-use-weighted runoff coefficients, and circular reinforced-concrete conduits were sized with the Manning equation. The catchment was delineated into two zones by topography and runoff concentration. Zone I (857.1 ha) requires a conveyance capacity of 0.63–1.57 m³/s and 1.86 km of closed channel, whereas Zone II (272.4 ha) requires 0.35–0.80 m³/s and 14.39 km. Circular conduits of 600–1200 mm diameter provide full-flow capacities of 0.43–2.76 m³/s at velocities of 1.5–2.4 m/s, satisfying the self-cleansing range while remaining below the scouring limit. Field observation confirmed that inundation develops when rainfall persists beyond one hour in low-lying, obstructed reaches. The main novelty of the study is a zone-specific, return-period-referenced closed circular drainage model in which conduits are placed beneath the road corridor, releasing surface land for urban functions while maintaining hydraulic efficiency and reducing sediment retention relative to the trapezoidal open channels currently in service.

papers.title: Multi-method estimation of groundwater recharge in the Fetam catchment, Upper Blue Nile Basin, Ethiopia
papers.summary: Reliable groundwater resources are essential in catchments characterized by strong rainfall seasonality and intermittent surface-water availability, such as the Fetam catchment in the Upper Blue Nile Basin, Ethiopia. In this study, groundwater recharge was quantified using a multi-method approach to reduce method-dependent uncertainty and provide a defensible recharge range for sustainable groundwater management. Five independent methods were applied: soil moisture balance, baseflow separation of streamflow, chloride mass balance, water-table fluctuation, and catchment water balance. Hydro-meteorological data, groundwater-level measurements, hydrochemical analyses, land use, soil, and hydrogeological information were integrated and spatially aggregated using Thiessen polygon weighting. Mean annual recharge estimates varied from 112.7 ± 2.2 to 244.9 ± 12.4 mm/year, corresponding to approximately 6.5–14% of mean annual rainfall. Higher recharge values were obtained from baseflow separation and water-table fluctuation methods, reflecting strong seasonal groundwater responses. In contrast, soil-moisture balance and water-balance methods yielded lower estimates because they explicitly accounted for evapotranspiration and runoff losses. The chloride mass balance method produced intermediate values and represents longer-term effective recharge. Recharge was found to be highly seasonal and spatially heterogeneous, with highland areas acting as major recharge zones and lowland areas functioning mainly as discharge zones. Overall, convergence among multiple methods suggests a realistic recharge range of approximately 165–220.1 mm/year for the Fetam catchment. The study demonstrates that multi-method recharge assessment is essential in data-limited, seasonally dry basins and provides a scientific basis for sustainable groundwater development and drought-resilient water management.

papers.title: THE STABILITY OF SOIL-ROCK MIXTURE SLOPES UNDER COMBINED EFFECTS OF RAINFALL AND TUNNEL EXCAVATION
papers.source: Eurasia Journal of Science and Technology
papers.summary: Because of their heterogeneous composition, soil-rock mixture (SRM) slopes respond strongly to both rainfall infiltration and tunnel excavation. In the model test, heavy rainfall was applied while two tunnels were excavated, and water content, deformation, and earth pressure were monitored continuously. Settlement accumulated rapidly at the beginning of the test as infiltration increased the soil mass weight and reduced shear strength. The subsequent increase became slower with further excavation. Lateral displacement, by contrast, showed a distinct sudden change before entering a period of gradual development. Earth pressure passed through three stages: relative stability, rapid change, and subsequent adjustment. The test results show that rainfall-induced weakening and excavation-related stress redistribution acted together to control the slope response, providing experimental support for stability assessment under similar conditions.

papers.title: Visualization Design and Effect Simulation of Reservoir Slope Reinforcement Scheme Based on 3D GIS
papers.source: International Journal of Grid and High Performance Computing
papers.summary: Reservoir slope engineering is often affected by various factors, such as rainfall infiltration. The traditional reliance on two-dimensional drawings and profile analysis has obvious limitations in identifying high-risk areas and coordinating the layout of reinforcement schemes. In this study, an integrated expression platform with a three-dimensional geographic information system was constructed, and the design idea of parametric visualization of a reinforcement scheme was proposed. According to the stability performance, displacement response characteristics, and the shrinkage law of risk area, a systematic comparative analysis is carried out of each reinforcement scheme under different working conditions. The deep integration of a three-dimensional geographic information system's spatial expression and reinforcement design was realized, and a complete closed loop of identification, design, verification, and optimization was constructed, which provides more intuitive and reliable technical support for design and communication for reservoir slope engineering.

papers.title: Remote Sensing and GIS-Based Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in the Eastern Region of Ghana Using Analytical Hierarchy Process
Advanced Hydro-Geospatial Modeling for Groundwater Potential Zoning in the Baro River Watershed: Geographic Information System and Remote Sensing Approach
papers.summary: Groundwater is vital for ecosystems and livelihoods in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in Ethiopia, dubbed the “water tower of Africa.” Despite its significance, many areas face water scarcity due to data scarcity and an uneven distribution of resources. The Baro River watershed, covering over 23,000 km2 in Southwestern Ethiopia, poses a critical study area that has been largely overlooked. A hydro-geospatial modeling framework, utilizing remote sensing (RS), Geographic Information Systems (GIS), and Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) via the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP), was employed to map Groundwater Potential Zones (GWPZ) across the region. Nine environmental parameters were assessed for their impact on groundwater recharge, with rainfall as the primary influencer. The analysis involved reclassifying and weighting each factor, yielding a Consistency Ratio (CR) of 0.067, well below the acceptable threshold of <0.10, indicating reliable results. The resulting groundwater potential map classified zones into five categories: very high, high, moderate, low, and very low potential. High-potential zones are predominantly located in the Gambella lowlands, benefiting from favorable groundwater infiltration conditions in fractured volcanic and alluvial deposits. In contrast, low-potential areas correspond to steep slopes with dense drainage. The findings reveal significant groundwater development opportunities, with over 90% of the watershed exhibiting moderate to very high potential, suggesting effective water management strategies through the integration of GIS and AHP for enhanced groundwater evaluation.

papers.title: Spatial analysis of LULC change and DEM-derived hydrological characteristics in a tropical micro-watershed (Lubuk Yu, Malaysia)
papers.source: Journal of tropical resources and sustainable science/Journal of Tropical Resources and Sustainable Science
papers.summary: Land use and land cover (LULC) change plays important role in influencing hydrological characteristics, especially in watersheds that are sensitive to both natural variability and anthropogenic disturbance. This study focuses on spatiotemporal LULC dynamics and examines terrain-derived hydrological characteristics in the Lubuk Yu watershed, Pahang, Malaysia (4.12 km²), using Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and remote sensing techniques. Multi-temporal Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager (OLI) imagery from 2016 and 2023 was classified using a supervised maximum likelihood approach into three dominant land cover classes: vegetation, water bodies, and barren land. The results indicate that vegetation cover decreased from 3.10 km² (75%) in 2016 to 2.80 km² (68%) in 2023, while water bodies increased from 0.78 km² (19%) to 1.01 km² (24%), and barren land increased from 0.24 km² (6%) to 0.29 km² (7%). Classification accuracy achieved 86.67% (Kappa = 0.77) for 2016 and 83.33% (Kappa = 0.74) for 2023, indicating substantial agreement with reference data. Hydrological characteristics derived from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) Digital Elevation Model (DEM) include watershed delineation, flow direction, flow accumulation, and stream ordering. Morphometric analysis indicates a drainage density of 28.64 km km⁻² and stream frequency of 29.78 streams km⁻², reflecting a dense and responsive headwater drainage system dominated by first-order streams (62 channels) with a total stream length of 68.34 km. Spatial overlay analysis reveals that areas experiencing vegetation reduction are frequently associated with zones of higher flow accumulation, particularly along tributary corridors, suggesting increased potential for runoff concentration. This study provides a process-oriented interpretation of how moderate land-cover changes in a tropical micro-watershed can be linked to terrain-controlled hydrological behaviour. The findings offer baseline insights to support wate

papers.title: Prediction of Unsaturated Hydraulic Conductivity of Cement-stabilised Laterite Soil under Climate-Induced Wetting and Drying Cycles
papers.summary: Climate change, characterised by rising temperatures and changing precipitation patterns, significantly impacts the geotechnical behaviour of soil. This includes alterations in soil’s shear strength, compressibility, and permeability, which in turn affect soil structure and its ability to manage water absorption and retention. Increasing soil moisture can generally reduce permeability by filling finer pores and decreasing pore system connectivity. However, the impact of unsaturated conditions on the soil’s permeability is often overlooked in design compared to saturated conditions. Hence, changes in temperature and rainfall patterns may affect water infiltration into the soil, potentially reducing groundwater recharge and increasing flood risks. Johor, Malaysia, has extensive tropical soil coverage (tropical region), which serves as the focus of this study. Hence, the research aims to elucidate how climate change influences both unstabilised and cement-stabilised laterite soils’ permeability by conducting the falling head permeability tests to determine saturated hydraulic conductivity (ksat), while unsaturated hydraulic conductivity (kunsat) is derived using GeoStudio (SEEP/W) based on experimental data from soil-water characteristic curve (SWCC) and ksat under varying matric suctions. Results indicate that both saturated and unsaturated conditions significantly affect the permeability coefficient of unstabilised and cement-stabilised laterite soils, with the substantial reduction in permeability largely attributed to the effect of saturation and stabiliser. Thus, predicting unsaturated permeability coefficients in the context of climate change is crucial for effective disaster management, as it will improves infrastructure design, enhances risk assessments, and supports community preparedness, ultimately fostering more resilient societies capable of withstanding the challenges of a changing climate.

papers.title: Organoclay containing filtration systems as nature based solutions to treat PAHs in road runoff
papers.summary: Combined impact of increasing impermeable surfaces in urban areas and elevated occurrence of high intensity rainfalls due to climate change results in higher urban runoff. This urban runoff transports Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs), frequently emitted from vehicles and accumulated on impermeable urban surfaces such as roads or parking lots and causes spread of these contaminants among many others. PAHs as persistent and bioaccumulative priority organic pollutants end up in surface water, groundwater, or soil environments degrading their quality. Therefore, controlling pollutants at the source is considered the best long-term solution. On-site filtration systems can be deployed as Nature Based Solutions (NBS) to remove pollutants from urban runoff and protect receiving water bodies in addition to their other benefits like climate change mitigation or adaptation. Clay minerals in filter media might serve to remove ionic and polar pollutants but they are ineffective in treating nonionic PAHs. Indeed, their percentage in a filter is limited due to their low hydraulic conductivity. On the other hand, organoclays which are synthesized by integrating surfactants into clay structure are found successful to reduce PAH concentrations without interfering with the hydraulic conductivity of the filter. So, in this study filter columns consisting of sand and organoclay (HDTMA-bentonite) (4:1) are operated under dynamic conditions for a month. Synthetic road runoff is prepared with 5 of the most commonly observed PAHs in dissolved phase of road runoff (Naphthalene (NAP), Acenaphthene (ACE), Phenanthrene (PHE), Fluoranthene (FLA) and Pyrene (PYR)), heavy metals, and ammonium. This synthetic road runoff is pumped through the filter continuously and effluent concentrations of PAHs are determined by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). The results showed that removal performance is higher than 94%, 88% and 76% at initial concentrations of 100, 50 and 25 μg/L (of each

papers.title: Hydrochemistry of two headwater peatlands affected by deep gullies in the Maloti Mountains of Lesotho
Urbanization-Induced Groundwater Contamination in Barjisiyah Area, Southern Iraq: Hydrochemical, Isotopic, and Microbial Assessment
papers.summary: Recent urbanization and overexploitation have significantly degraded groundwater quality in the shallow unconfined aquifer in Barjisiyah. The study area is located within the discharge area and is exposed to natural salinization from the underlying layer and anthropogenic sources with limited rainfall recharge. Six groundwater samples have been collected from the unconfined aquifer across urbanized zones. Total Dissolved Solids reach an extremely high level of 22,200 mg/L, with a wide range of major ion concentrations. Hydrochemical facies are dominated by sodium-chloride and calcium-chloride, confirming advanced mineralization. The distinct geochemical and isotopic contents observed in the shallow aquifer suggest a conceptual mechanism of upward leakage from the underlying semi-confined layer. The evaporitic minerals are dominant, with no halite dissolution, sulfate mineral saturation, and supersaturation of carbonate minerals. The isotopic signatures have been plotted below the Global and regional Meteoric Water Lines, with recognized negative values of d-excess, providing dual insights into the hydrogeological processes governing the aquifer. Isotopic signatures suggest infiltration of evaporated water into the aquifer and upward saline mixing. The major finding is that the microbial indicator counts exceed the levels set by global safety standards, with E. coli reaching 400 CFU/mL. Groundwater quality deterioration may increasingly limit agricultural suitability over time.

papers.title: The effect of stormwater infiltration shallow urban groundwater quality: a case study in the Cape Flats, South Africa
papers.summary: Cape Town, South Africa, is diversifying its water supply in line with its commitment to becoming a water sensitive city (WSC). Blue-green infrastructure (BGI) is key to the implementation of a WSC and can assist in restoring the pre-development hydrological cycle and improving water quality. Approximately 200 stormwater detention ponds overlie the Cape Flats Aquifer and serve as flood control measures, but are very often vacant open spaces, at risk of becoming dumping grounds or informal settlements. One of these detention ponds has been transformed into a multifunctional BGI with stormwater harvesting via infiltration and this case study evaluated the impact of this on groundwater quality over a period of two years. After accounting for dilution effects, the mean contaminant removal during infiltration for ammonium, total organic carbon, total dissolved phosphate, aluminium and zinc were 92%, 84%, 92%, 83%, and 91% respectively. Results also indicated that denitrification of the groundwater is occurring.

papers.title: Влияние гидрологических факторов на разработку Тюбегатанского месторождения калийных солей (Республика Узбекистан)
papers.summary: The development of the Tyubegatan potash deposit, characterized by a complex tectonic environment, inevitably faces a number of factors affecting safety and organization of the production process. One of these is the occurrence of emergency water seepage in the workings, caused by precipitation infiltrating through the cover deposits via systems of vertical fractures. The intensity and frequency of these water seepage events are related, among other factors, to the hydrological and hydrochemical characteristics of surface water bodies in the area of the deposit’s mining allotment. Hydrological calculations allowed us to estimate the long-term average surface water inflow from the catchment area near the primary mining site, which amounted to 43 m³/h. Maximum water inflows (over 180 m³/h) were recorded in early June 2012 and late May 2018 and coincided with rare rain floods. Hydrochemical studies, including laboratory analysis, showed that the total mineralization of most streams and springs in the study area (1-10 g/L) is significantly lower than that of mine waters (over 300 g/L). This indicates active dissolution of salt-containing rocks. To minimize surface water infiltration into the mine workings, deepening and straightening work is proposed to create a channel for the Tyushsay River downstream along the entire length of the mining allotment. To prevent emergencies resulting from a sharp increase in surface runoff infiltration caused by heavy rainfall, the implementation of continuous automated monitoring of hydrometeorological parameters is recommended.

papers.title: Slope Stability Analysis of Highway Embankments Under Extreme Rainfall Conditions
papers.source: International Journal of Frontline Research in Engineering and Technology
papers.summary: The structural integrity of highway embankments, engineered cut slopes, and natural hillsides is an essential concern for geotechnical professionals and civil engineers worldwide. Failures along transport corridors frequently lead to catastrophic ground movements, extensive infrastructure damage, economic paralysis, and significant risk to human life(Aktas et al., 2025). Over several decades, numerous analytical and computational procedures have been formulated to quantify slope equilibrium. These computational techniques differ substantially in their underlying theoretical assumptions spanning classic limit equilibrium formulations, progressive failure mechanisms, and finite element deformation analyses as well as in their implementation via design charts or numerical simulation packages (Ikeagwuani & Nwonu, 2023). Despite these operational differences, all methods evaluate safety margins by establishing a global Factor of Safety or by comparing mobilized driving stresses directly against the available shear strength envelope of the soil mass. In highway construction, various stabilization and slope reinforcement techniques are deployed, each distinguished by installation complexity, long-term durability, and overall project cost (Xu & Zhang, 2025). The primary aim of this paper is to investigate slope stability across artificial transportation embankments and natural formations, placing special emphasis on extreme hydrological conditions and parameter sensitivity within limit equilibrium models (Utepov et al., 2022). This analytical exploration aims to refine predictive capabilities, optimize geotechnical design practices, and guide the deployment of resilient engineering countermeasures along modern transport networks (Sharma & Shrivastava, 2025).

papers.title: Slope Stability Analysis Against Landslides Using the Bishop Method (Case Study: Katapop II, Salawati District, Sorong Regency)
papers.summary: Sorong Regency has hilly and mountainous topography, making it prone to landslides, especially on steep slopes during periods of high rainfall. Landslides in this area can damage infrastructure and threaten human safety. These conditions highlight the importance of slope stability analysis to identify potential landslides and mitigation efforts to minimize disaster impacts. This study aims to analyze slope stability under saturated and unsaturated conditions and to determine the soil characteristics in Katapop II, Sorong Regency. The method used was the Bishop method utilizing GeoStudio software and manual calculations to validate the Safety Factor (SF) values. Based on the calculation results, the slopes in Katapop II were categorized as unstable under saturated conditions, with safety factors (SF) of 0.798 from the software analysis and 0.53 from manual calculations. Under unsaturated conditions, the safety factors (SF) were 2.69 from the software analysis and 2.70 from manual calculations, indicating stable conditions. The soil characteristics were identified as clay according to the AASHTO classification system, inorganic clay according to the USCS classification system, and silt loam according to the USDA classification system.

papers.title: CRITIQUE OF VETIVER ENGINEERING AND INTEGRATED SLOPE STABILIZATION IN THE HIMALAYA
papers.source: Quantum Journal of Engineering Science and Technology
papers.summary: This review critically examines the role of Vetiver grass (Chrysopogon zizanioides) in Himalayan slope stabilization and the emergence of what the authors term Vetiver Engineering the monocultural, geotechnically unsupported deployment of Vetiver as a standalone slope stabilization solution. Drawing upon a systematic synthesis of geotechnical, ecological, hydrological, and policy literature, this paper evaluates where Vetiver is mechanistically effective, where it is structurally inadequate, and why its uncritical proliferation in Nepal and adjacent Himalayan regions represents a critical gap between evidence and practice. Vetiver provides measurable benefits for surface erosion control and shallow root reinforcement in cohesive soils, but it cannot substitute for geotechnical drainage, structural reinforcement, or discontinuity-controlled failure analysis in complex Himalayan terrain. Integrated bioengineering approaches combining geotechnical screening, hydrological control, structural reinforcement, and mixed species vegetation are demonstrated to deliver more resilient, cost-effective, and ecologically sustainable outcomes. The paper synthesizes engineering perspectives, root mechanics, regional case evidence, material durability data, comparative performance analyses, and critiques of Vetiver Engineering institutional drivers. It proposes a stepwise integrated design framework, standardized monitoring protocols, and a policy reform agenda. The conclusion calls for evidence-based procurement reform, interdisciplinary research, and regional knowledge-sharing to guide Himalayan slope management in an era of increasing climate driven rainfall intensity and seismicity.

Analysis the Characteristics and Performance of Polyethersulfone-Carbon Nanotube Membranes Fabricated Using Electric Field Method for Water Filtration Applications
papers.summary: This study aims to address the effect of Carbon Nanotube (CNT) addition on the characteristics and performance of polyethersulfone (PES) membranes fabricated using the Electric Field method. Four PES membranes were fabricated with addition of CNT and denoted as SM0 (0% CNT), SM1 (0.5% CNT), SM2 (1% CNT), and SM3 (1.5% CNT). SEM observations showed average pore sizes of 0.62±0.12 μm to 0.82±0.18 μm, and AFM images showed the ability of CNTs to increase topographical complexity. The tensile test results indicated that addition of CNT increased the tensile strength of the membrane. The TGA and DTG test graphs showed that addition of CNT can increase the thermal resistance of the membrane. FTIR spectra were in agreement with characteristic PES functional groups. The XRD data showed that the amorphous nature remains dominant, indicating that this composite membrane successfully combines the mechanical strength and functional properties of CNTs without sacrificing the intrinsic pore structure of the PES polymer. Addition of CNT to the membrane increased its hydrophilicity, as evidenced by decrease in water contact angle on the membrane. Addition of CNT can also increase the membrane permeability, as indicated by an increase in the membrane permeability values in the range of 1 to 6 bar. In terms of durability, adding CNT to the membrane can increase its durability, meaning that membranes with added CNT can last longer than pure PES membranes.

papers.title: Microstructure and Texture Regulation of Industrial-Scale Planar Flow Cast Fe–3.8 Pct Si Ultra-Thin Non-Oriented Electrical Steel Strips by Two-Step Cold Rolling–Annealing
Unravelling the tectonic and climatic controls on Upper Jurassic mass flow deposits in NE Scotland
papers.summary: The NE Scottish coast between Portgower and Navidale contains an unusual succession of interbedded boulder beds and fine-grained rocks of upper Kimmeridgian to Tithonian (Upper Jurassic) age that have attracted attention for over 150 years. Their juxtaposition next to the Helmsdale Fault has commonly led to the inference that their deposition is entirely fault controlled and shows no systematic ordering. This study presents: the first centimetre-scale reproducible graphic log of this c. 4.3 Ma (610 m) sedimentary succession; new palynomorph biostratigraphy; detailed facies analysis; sketch maps; new ammonite finds and drone footage. The new biostratigraphical data considerably refines four of the seven boundaries. Furthermore, palynology proves the scitulus and hudlestoni zones, and ammonites the elegans zone, in NE Scotland for the first time. Together the data show that the succession is a bimodal system of five fine-grained facies (tiger stripe) and five coarse-grained facies, that it is stratigraphically fairly complete and there are no major faults that remove stratigraphy. Sediment transport was mostly fault parallel. Sequence stratigraphical analysis shows 67 metre-scale cycles interpreted as parasequences and eight depositional sequences that are typically 60-70 metres thick. Parasequences comprise coarsening-upward micro-turbidite packages (composed of tiger stripe facies) usually capped by a pebble-cobble or pebble-boulder debris flow. Sequences comprise a falling stage systems tract of stacked pebble-cobble debris flows or high-density turbidites, a lowstand systems tract where the facies are highly variable laterally and a transgressive systems tract and highstand systems tract, both composed of generally well-developed parasequences. The sequence boundaries are always sharp and some show erosion. The maximum rate of relative sea-level rise is marked by a maximum flooding zone of fine-grained micro turbidites and hemipelagic facies. These cycles suggest

papers.title: Dates, locations, and local meteorological conditions associated with non-eruptive debris flows on Mount Shasta from 1900-2025
papers.summary: This dataset contains dates, geographic locations, and meteorological data associated with non-eruptive debris flows on Mount Shasta. A non-eruptive debris flow an alternate term for volcanic mudflow or lahar. This dataset was derived from existing scientific literature, historical California newspaper records, and open-access weather and climate data.

papers.title: Time-lapse images for debris flow monitoring at Mount Shasta, California in 2022
papers.summary: Over the summer of 2022 the USGS deployed temporary seismometers, infrasound arrays, and cameras along several drainages at Mount Shasta, California. Twenty-one debris flows were confirmed by the cameras or other observations. This data set consists of images from cameras placed near three drainages (Bolam Creek, Mud Creek, and Whitney Creek). Images were stored on internal Secure Digital (SD) cards and real-time thumbnail images were broadcast via cell modem for real-time monitoring. Time intervals between images were toggled remotely and range from 30 seconds to 10 minutes and images were only collected during daylight hours. The images for each camera are contained in one to three zipped folders (marked as a, b, and c in chronological order), corresponding to SD cards removed from the cameras when full. A separate zipped folder (GIFs) contains daily animations from 0700 PDT and selected debris flows seen at each camera during their operation. Images with identifiable people have been removed.

papers.title: Supplemental Material: Erosion and sediment transfer by debris flows on Miocene intrashelf clinoforms, offshore New Jersey, USA
papers.summary: Figures S1–S7 provide additional seismic time slices, seismic profiles, maps, and supporting interpretations of the geomorphic features described in the main text.

papers.title: Assessing Geomorphic Effects of Hurricane Hilary, CA 2023
papers.summary: In August 2023, Hurricane Hilary brought widespread heavy rainfall to Southern California. Some normally arid desert areas received more than their typical annual rainfall, which triggered debris flows, flash floods, and large-scale sediment movement. Lidar data was collected shortly after the storm to capture evidence of how the landscape changed during this event. This project and its research is being conducted within the structure of the Center for Land Surface Hazards (CLaSH). Its goal is to document erosion, deposition, impacts on infrastructure, and to improve understanding of cascading hazards. The data also support the development and testing of next-generation hazard models.

papers.title: Volumetric Water Content and Shear Failure of Volcanic Ash: Evidence From Powder Shear Cell Analyses
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Volcanic debris flows are among the most hazardous mass-movement processes because they are unpredictable and can rapidly attain high velocities and destructive power, causing fatalities and damage to buildings and infrastructure. Their initiation and propagation are controlled by a combination of predisposing conditions (topography, catchment morphology, geological/structural setting, etc.) and transient hydrological forcing. Water is often the key agent because it modifies the effective stress state of the soil and can favor excess pore-pressure buildup, thereby directly affecting shear strength. In this study, we investigated how increasing water content modifies the mechanical behavior of three ash-rich soils collected in the Sarno area (Campanian Volcanic Province, Southern Italy). The deposits were tested at volumetric water content values from 0 to 8 percent in 2 percent increments through undrained shear experiments performed with a rheometer under controlled conditions. The results indicate the onset of matric-suction effects associated with water-meniscus formation as the material transitions from dry to moist conditions, accompanied by an initial increase in apparent cohesion and a shift in flow behavior from a free-flowing granular response to a markedly cohesive regime. These results improve the knowledge about the influence of the moisture content on the mechanical stability of volcanic ash soils, providing constraints for predictive modeling and hazard mitigation in volcanic terrains.

papers.title: Disentangling seismic and hydroclimatic controls on long-term debris-flow activity in the eastern Tibetan Plateau
papers.summary: Historical records substantially underestimate debris-flow activity in remote mountain catchments, limiting understanding of its long-term seismic and hydroclimatic controls. We combined dendrogeomorphic reconstruction, multi-temporal remote sensing, post-earthquake decay modelling, and structural equation path analysis to investigate debris-flow activity in six adjacent catchments of Shuangqiao Gully, eastern Tibetan Plateau. Based on 1,098 growth disturbances from 164 fir trees, we reconstructed 175 catchment-year debris-flow records, extending the chronology to 1916. Individual catchments had mean recurrence intervals of 2.7–3.4 years. During the common period 1953-2025, tree rings identified 159 catchment-year records, whereas only 12 events were documented historically. Debris-flow activity and bare-ground exposure increased markedly after the nearby 1989 Suoluozhai and large 2008 Wenchuan earthquakes, while the distant 2013 Lushan earthquake produced little short-term response. Estimated recovery times varied from 5.7 to 17.3 years among catchments. Flood-season precipitation and the annual number of days with precipitation ≥5 mm showed the strongest statistically significant correlations with activity (r=0.40 and 0.37, p<0.001 and p<0.01, respectively). Activity also increased with drought–flood abrupt alternation (r=0.35, p=0.002), which reflects the temporal structure of flood-season rainfall independently of its total amount, whereas ENSO phases showed no clear differences. The path model explained 40% of the interannual variation in active-channel proportion. Flood-season precipitation contributed 41.6% of the normalized effect magnitude, followed by drought–flood abrupt alternation (33.3%), earthquakes (23.2%), and ENSO (1.9%). These results show that hydroclimatic conditions dominate interannual debris-flow activity, while earthquakes generate transient susceptibility that can persist for more than a decade and differs substantially among adjacent catch

papers.title: Seasonal influence on post-fire debris flow likelihood after the 2020 Lake Fire
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: The increasing severity of wildfires in Western North America is widely hypothesized to lead to an increase in the likelihood of post-fire debris flows (PFDF), specifically those triggered by high-intensity rain. PFDF likelihoods are highest in the first year and tend to decrease over time. However, it is not well understood how seasonal variation affects PFDF initiation in the years following a fire. Here, we investigated how different physical parameters influence seasonal PFDF likelihood, informed by four years of field and satellite observations from the 2020 Lake Fire in Southern California. We found that unsaturated hydraulic conductivity was an order of magnitude greater during the dry season than during the wet season, significantly reducing the PFDF likelihood. Our simulations show that vegetation cover has less of an impact on PFDF likelihood than hydraulic conductivity or grain size. This study helps clarify the relative importance of hydraulic conductivity, grain size, and vegetation on PFDF as these parameters vary seasonally and evolve over four years after the fire. Our results suggest that seasonal variation plays a major role in determining PFDF likelihood and therefore, climatic and seasonal patterns need to be considered in future field and modeling studies.

Across a circle of 700 km radius, about 1.54 million km², it would produce about 674 TWh of solar electricity a year and keep 4 to 10 billion m³ of rainwater. That electricity equals the annual output of about 92 one-gigawatt nuclear reactors. The water equals a major river, assembled from storm runoff that today mostly evaporates. The conventional approach builds these capacities separately: a power station here, a dam there, flood channels, a wetland reserve and a groundwater programme, each with its own land, crews, controls and owners. Godmode's thesis is that much of that duplication can be avoided. When a canal is also a flood channel, a habitat corridor and a solar mount, one unit of spending does several jobs. This blueprint calls that saving the integration dividend. Edition 4.0 takes the dividend down to ground level. VerdantVolt bifacial solar turf is a roll-out surface that generates electricity, holds battery storage and routes rain through micro-channels in its base. Where earlier editions put solar over water, turf makes the solar field itself part of the water system. Each square metre of turf is a power plant, a battery site and a catchment apron at once. papers.title: Development of Solar Pump and IoT Monitoring in Polluted Areas for Enhancing Clean Water Access
papers.summary: Water plays a vital role in human life. However, access to clean water can be a challenge in rural and polluted areas, where groundwater quality is declining due to environmental pollution, followed by limited access and high costs. To address this issue, this study presents a solar-powered water-pumping system integrated with IoT power and water monitoring for access to clean water. The proposed work has several contributions. First, it builds a battery-less solar panel pump system along with procedures to minimize operating and maintenance costs. Second, it modifies the filter on a brushless DC pump to strengthen the component's resistance to small sediments. Third, it implements integrated power monitoring and water distribution to meet domestic needs, water storage, and rice field irrigation. The solar panel system has a capacity of 4400 Wp to operate a 3000 W submersible pump and to provide real-time monitoring of water quality parameters through the Blynk platform. The analysis and evaluation results show that the system can operate stably at a DC bus voltage of 367 V and successfully discharge 15 m3/hour of water, with a water tank filling time of 30 minutes. The 20-mesh polyethylene filtration system can filter out small rock sediments that could damage the impeller. The IoT devices serve as electric load monitoring and an early warning mechanism against localized pollution. The integration of battery-less solar pumps, supported by filtration systems and monitoring devices, can be a reference model to address challenges in rural or ecologically vulnerable areas.

papers.title: Event Reconstruction and Hydroclimatic–Cryospheric Context of the 2018 Badswat Debris Flow–River Blockage, Pakistan
papers.summary: High Mountain Asia is undergoing rapid warming, with consequences for snow, ground thermal conditions, runoff, sediment availability, and water-related mass-movement hazards. This study combines watershed-scale hydroclimatic and cryospheric diagnostics with an event-scale reconstruction of the 17 July 2018 Badswat debris flow–river blockage in Gilgit–Baltistan, Pakistan. Snow-cover area (MODIS MOD10A1; 2000–2025), surface frost-number terrain (MODIS MOD11A2; 2001–2025), air temperature (ERA5-Land; 1950–2025), and precipitation (CHIRPS; 1981–2025) were analyzed in Google Earth Engine. The event was reconstructed in RAMMS-DF with Voellmy–Salm rheology (μ = 0.09, ξ = 500 m s−2) on a 12.5 m grid. Air temperature increased by 0.13 °C decade−1 (p < 0.001). Snow-cover and permafrost-favorable extents were negatively associated with temperature (r = −0.74 and −0.78), but neither showed a significant temporal trend over the shorter satellite record. CHIRPS precipitation increased by 1.7 mm yr−1 (p < 0.001), mainly in summer, although its annual variability agreed poorly with ERA5-Land and the trend is therefore product-specific. The calibrated scenario reproduced the mapped runout path, river-blockage location, and depositional zone, and yielded maxima of 15.17 m flow height, 33.82 m s−1 velocity, 2544 kPa impact pressure, and 81 kPa basal shear stress, with about 352,540 m3 of deposition. Because dynamic outputs lack independent measurements and joint parameter uncertainty was not quantified, they are scenario estimates rather than design values. The study provides an uncertainty-explicit event reconstruction and separates long-term environmental context from the unresolved event-scale trigger.

papers.title: The Effect of Erosion-Induced Amplification and Topographic Controls on the Evolution and Deposition of the 5 August 2016 Xiaosha River Debris-Flow Event in Yunnan, China
papers.summary: Channel erosion and sediment entrainment amplify rainstorm-triggered debris flows, but their interaction with topographic constraints remains poorly quantified. To reveal the controlling mechanism of erosion amplification on the disaster-forming process of rainstorm-type debris flows, using the 2016 Zhangba Xiaosha River event in Yunnan, China, we reconstructed debris-flow motion, erosion, and deposition with RAMMS::DEBRISFLOW. Five bed-erosion scenarios (0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75 and 1.0 m) were used to assess changes in deposit thickness, runout, velocity, impact pressure, and volume amplification. The 1.0 m baseline scenario successfully reproduced the observed path, depositional extent, and representative deposit thickness. Increasing the equivalent erosion depth from 0 to 1.0 m increased the total debris-flow volume from 2.0 × 104 to 4.27 × 104 m3, yielding an amplification factor of 2.14; without erosion, maximum runout was 44.2% shorter. Along-channel erosion supply increases the mass, flow depth and momentum of the moving mass, forming an amplification chain of “sediment supply−scale amplification−momentum maintenance−frontal propagation”. Feedback may exist between actual erosion intensity, flow velocity and flow depth, but the equivalent erosion depth in RAMMS scenarios in this study is a predefined parameter. Topography exerted reach-specific controls: steep upstream channels promoted initiation and acceleration, the middle reach dominated erosional bulking, and the wider, gentler downstream reach enhanced dissipation and deposition. Within the erosion scenarios of 0.75–1.0 m set in this study, when the equivalent erosion depth increased further, the newly entrained sediment mainly increased deposit thickness and inundation extent, while the increment of maximum runout distance was limited. The event disaster scale resulted from coupled erosion-induced amplification and longitudinal topographic constraints. Hazard assessments should integrate initial initiation

The impact of fires on permafrost: A case study of the Shestakovka River basin in Siberia using a one-dimensional mathematical model
papers.summary: Permafrost regions are vulnerable to forest fires that are increasing under global warming. This study presents the results of field experiments and mathematical modeling of short-term (one hour) forest fires. The experimental site Levaya Shestakovka (Central Yakutia, Russia) has been used as example. Three fire experiments were conducted using logs of Siberian larch and Scots pine which serve as a basis for the mathematical model. The model is based on solving the one-dimensional Stefan problem with unsaturated soil filtration and accounting for snow cover. The lower boundary condition is the geothermal heat flux, while the upper boundary condition is the heat exchange with the atmosphere. The field experiments show that only 8 percent of the heat from the fire has penetrated into the soil, which is supported by our model that indicates no significant effect on heat and mass transfer processes from short-term forest fires into permafrost. The research indicates that the contribution of short–lived forest fires to ground temperature changes is negligible; the heatwave penetrated only 0.5 m into the ground. Modeling showed that short-term forest fires have no significant effect on heat and mass transfer processes in permafrost. Thus, the research results indicate that low-severity forest fire regimes are not significant for permafrost thawing processes.

UNSATURATED SOIL MECHANICS APPROACH TO FORENSIC SPOOROLOGY
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Traditional forensic spoorology and trackway age estimation methodologies rely almost exclusively on macroclimatic weathering indices—specifically wind velocity, ambient precipitation, temperature fluctuations, and direct solar radiation—to model the degradation of human footprints. While the foundational Track Erosion Computation introduced by Cunningham (2011) brilliantly captures macro-weather and surface distortion, it can be significantly expanded by accounting for the sub-surface phase shifts occurring within soil micro-pores during environmental convergence with the atmospheric dew point. This paper introduces a novel cross-disciplinary mathematical model integrating unsaturated soil mechanics with forensic tracking. Scientific Status: This work is explicitly established as a proposed theoretical framework that requires rigorous empirical field testing and validation within appropriate environmental and geotechnical testing areas. By leveraging the Kelvin equation and the principles of matric suction, we demonstrate that when ambient temperature matches the dew point (T = T_d), water vapor undergoes capillary condensation directly inside the soil matrix prior to open-air dew formation. This phase change initiates a bimodal erosion path: an initial "Maximum Lock" phase driven by apparent cohesion, followed by a total "Saturation Slump" failure. Furthermore, we define a geometric boundary phenomenon termed the Top-Down Crest Avalanche, wherein localized moisture-suction gradients pull condensed liquid downward from the exposed upper crests of a footprint wall, inducing micro-shear failure along the trackway perimeter. This volume establishes the title, comprehensive literature review, and historical background necessary to ground this theory in the established physical sciences.

papers.summary: Abstract. Artificial drainage is widely used in agricultural landscapes to improve trafficability and prevent waterlogging, but comes at the expense of groundwater storage and regional drought resilience. Through model scenarios, this study evaluates how large-scale drain-level adjustments influence groundwater dynamics, water balances, and streamflow extremes across different regions in Flanders, Belgium. A physically based, spatially distributed hydrological model coupling land-surface and groundwater processes was adapted to represent controlled drainage through adjustable weirs, by modifying drain levels and incorporating temporary water storage within drainage ditches behind control structures. Permanently raising drain levels from 1 m to 0.5 m below the surface increased average groundwater levels by 15 cm across Flanders, with increases exceeding 30 cm in actively drained areas. Higher groundwater availability generally resulted in modest increases in evapotranspiration, particularly in flat sandy regions. Simulations showed that raising drain levels shortly after winter (April) was more effective than implementing measures only during summer (June onward), when groundwater tables had often already fallen below the drainage depth. Drainage management also altered streamflow extremes. Under a permanent drain-level increase, low flows increased by 12.8 %. In contrast, summer-only management reduced low flows by up to 10.1 % in some drainage-dominated catchments, highlighting a trade-off between local water retention and downstream water availability. The effects on flood peaks were spatially variable. Peak discharges increased by up to 11.3 % in saturation-prone areas due to reduced unsaturated soil storage, whereas temporary storage behind control structures reduced peak flows by up to 26.5 % in regions dominated by infiltration-excess runoff. The results demonstrate that drainage management can be an effective tool for increasing groundwater storage and mitig

papers.title: Stress regime in compacted fills during wetting and drying cycles under laterally restrained conditions
papers.summary: Climate change in the form of global warming is taking place. The impact of it on society is severe and unpredictable. The most noticeable evidences are: rise in land and sea temperatures (in particular in summer time), rise in sea levels, and wet winter combined with flash flooding. Dry summers and wet winters are the main contributors to many of the natural disasters in the world, witnessed in the last few decades. These disasters are directly or indirectly associated with soils (i.e., ground) which immediately response to any climatic changes. Soil is also an integral part of the modern infrastructure such as embankments, retaining walls, sub-base for roads and railway tracks, and many more. These structures are often referred to as Geo-Infrastructure. The impacts of climate change on the infrastructure are far-reaching. Policy makers and practicing engineers are fully aware of the consequences of climate change and investing resources to develop adaptation technologies to limit the impact and reduce repair and maintenance costs. A particular case examined in this thesis referred to the performance of compacted clays placed behind retaining structures. Compacted soils are often unsaturated at the time of placement and their responses to climate change for example, wetting can be swelling/collapse and reduction in strength. These issues are also influenced by the compaction energy, compaction water content and soil type. Compacted soils placed in accordance with BS guidelines (i.e., engineered fills) could swell upon wetting. If such swelling is restricted (for example conditions behind retaining wall) the horizontal pressure in the compacted soil would increase, raising concern on the stability of the structure. However, if the wetting is cyclic (wetting after prolonged drying) then progressive build-up of stress can lead to eventual failure. The above aspect was investigated in laboratory-based research. Three distinctively different soils were considered: Kaoli

Parametric Evaluation of Key Constitutive Components in a Bounding Surface Model for Unsaturated Soils
papers.summary: The lack of consensus on appropriate formulations for effective stress, the soil-water characteristic curve (SWCC), and the critical-state void ratio has plagued the constitutive modeling of unsaturated soils. This paper presents a numerical parametric investigation of the aforementioned modeling components using a rate-independent hyperelastic bounding surface plasticity model for unsaturated granular soils. The constitutive model was calibrated against experimental results for a mid-Atlantic silty sand, and stress–strain and volumetric response simulations were conducted using alternative formulations for Bishop’s effective stress parameter, SWCC, and critical-state void ratio. The study indicated that the choice of SWCC has the greatest influence on model accuracy, particularly in predicting volumetric behavior, with formulations that employ more parameters providing greater fidelity. It was observed that variations in the definition of effective stress have a comparatively limited impact, whereas accurate representations of the critical-state void ratio improve overall predictive capability. The findings are based on a single silty sand, an SWCC estimated from grain size distribution data, monotonic loading conditions, and a limited critical-state database. Accordingly, the conclusions should be interpreted within the context of the investigated material, constitutive framework, and stress range considered. The findings highlight the relative importance of key modeling components and guide the selection and calibration of constitutive models for unsaturated soils.
